Document Title: Adaptation approaches in Danish municipalities' climate action plans (report on the DK2020 project)
Family Title: DK2020 Project
Family Summary:
The DK2020 project intends for every municipality to draw up a climate action plan to reduce emissions and help keep global heating at safe levels. The impact of this collective effort has huge potential – Danish municipalities aim to cut 76% of Denmark’s total emissions by 2030, compared to 1990.

DK2020 supports municipalities all over Denmark in developing, upgrading or adjusting their existing work on climate action to global best practice, and in ultimately developing climate action plans in line with the 1.5 degree goal in the Paris Agreement. The climate action plans must show the way towards local climate neutrality in 2050 – or sooner. 

The climate action plans will comply with the Climate Action Planning Framework developed by the C40 cities network. DK2020 marks the first time this international standard is adapted and applied for use in smaller cities and municipalities. Realdania, a private association in Denmark which supports projects in architecture and planning, formed a partnership with Local Government Denmark and the five Danish regions – ensuring DK2020 a total funding of DKK 45 mill (appr. €6 mio.) that made it possible to invite all Danish municipalities to join the project. Simultaneously, five geographical organizations with specialist competencies were established to provide advice and consultancy on a regional level. From the beginning in 2019, C40 and green think tank CONCITO have assisted as knowledge partners and project secretariat.

Document Title: Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Title: Belgium Updated Final National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP). 2021-2030
Family Summary:
The National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) is a ten-year integrated document mandated by the European Union to each of its member states in order for the EU to meet its overall greenhouse gases emissions targets. 

The plan aims to define measures adapted to different dimensions: 1) decarbonisation dimension: reduction of GHG emissions by 35% in 2030 compared to 2005 for non-ET sectors, a Belgian contribution of 17.4% of renewable energies compared to gross final energy consumption; 2) energy efficiency dimension : Belgium has set a contribution to the European target of 32.5% by 2030 (15% in primary energy and 12% in final energy); 3) energy security dimension : one of the most important challenges for Belgium, in the short and medium term. A radical shift in the electricity mix due to the planned gradual phase-out of nuclear power around 2025 is planned; 4) the internal energy market dimension : regarding energy transport infrastructure, efforts will be made in the coming years to strengthen the existing interconnections with France and the Netherlands; 5) research, Innovation and Competitiveness dimension : Belgium is committed to devoting at least 3% of its gross domestic product overall to RD.

Family Summary: This decree adopts Peru's National Strategy to Combat Desertification and Drought 2016-2030 into law.Peru's National Strategy to Combat Desertification and Drought 2016-2030 has six specific goals: (1) elaborate and update soil quality baselines to include the causes and consequences of desertification, land degradation and drought based on scientific and technological guidelines, (2) strengthen regulatory frameworks related to desertification, land degradation and drought in affected areas, (3) develop synergistic, multisectoral, intrasectoral, regional and local plans, programs and projects to reduce desertification, land degradation and the impact of drought in affected areas, (4) raise awareness of the problem and actions to mitigate desertification, land degradation and the impact of drought through the media, (5) strengthen management capacities of desertification, land degradation and drought in various interest groups on a scientific-technological basis, and (6) develop scientific research or technological innovations that help sustainable land management by taking advantage of traditional knowledge.There is a specific subsection (1.5.2) dedicated to the relationship between climate change and desertification in Peru.

Document Title: Flood Risk Act
Family Title: Flood Risk Act
Family Summary:
The Flood Risk Act (Act on the assessment and management of flood risk from watercourses and lakes) establish the framework for assessing and managing flood risk from watercourses and lakes with a view to reducing the negative consequences of floods for human health, the environment, cultural heritage and economic activities. It obligates municipalities with identified risk areas to prepare risk management plans. The Danish Coastal Authority is responsible for identifying risk areas based on a national assessment of the risk of flooding from sea and watercourses.

Denmark has a total of 14 risk areas identified pursuant to EU Directive 2007/60/EC on the assessment and management of flood risks. All 27 affected municipalities have drawn up risk management plans. The plans outline the actions that municipalities can take to prevent major devastation in the event of catastrophic flooding.

Document Title: One-page summary of the Global Climate Action Strategy
Family Title: A Green and Sustainable World - Global Climate Action Strategy
Family Summary:
The Danish Government’s new long-term strategy on global climate action sets the direction for Denmark’s international climate efforts. The aim is to:

  • Increase global climate ambition: Denmark will work to influence states and non-state actors to commit to ambitious objectives contributing to limiting global warming. It will work with States, multilateral organisations and civil society for ambitious efforts on climate adaptation, resilience and sustainable development.
  • Reduce global greenhouse gas emissions: Denmark will work for a global green transition focused on reducing emissions of large emitters and sustainable development in developing countries.
  • Strengthen focus on adaptation and sustainable development: Denmark wants to inspire and drive resilience and adaptation initiatives. It wants a far more climate-oriented development cooperation focused on climate change and sustainable development in the poorest and most fragile developing countries, and to spread Danish prevention and adaptation solutions globally.
  • Shift financial flows to green: Denmark will contribute to shifting global financial flows from fossil fuels to green, climate-friendly investments. It will support the greening of financial markets and the energy markets and systems designed to foster investments in renewables. It will also strive to increase the mobilisation of climate finance for the poorest and most fragile countries.
  • Cooperate with the private sector on green solutions: To drive successful global climate action, Denmark will work with the private sector to promote green Danish solutions globally, with exports providing a basis for increased green growth in Denmark.

Document Title: Climate Change Policy for the Coffee Subsector of Honduras
Family Title: Climate Change Policy for the Coffee Subsector of Honduras

Document Title: Council decision (2024) amending the implementing decision on the approval of the assessment of the recovery and resilience plan for Denmark in 2021
Family Title: Denmark's recovery and resilience plan
Family Summary:
To benefit from the support of the Recovery and Resilience Facility set up by the EU in the aftermath of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis, Member States submit their recovery and resilience plans to the European Commission. Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient. The Commission validates the plan after which it effectively enters in force and EU subsidies can start flowing towards the member state.The European Commission has given a positive assessment to Denmark’s recovery and resilience plan, which will be financed by €1.5 billion in grants. 59% of the plan’s total allocation for reforms and investments supports climate objectives, including:

  • Support for green transport: providing premiums for the scrapping of old diesel cars, building new bicycle paths, infrastructure for electric bicycles and support to purchase green ferries. €259 million
  • Investment window and green tax reform: temporarily increasing tax deduction for companies investing in technology and software to facilitate their transition to new business models with lower greenhouse gas emissions. €407 million
  • Green research and development projects: supporting public-private research cooperation to accelerate the development of climate-friendly technology solutions. €94 million
  • Replacing oil burners and gas furnaces: expanding district heating grids into new areas and providing support to households to convert to electric heat pump systems. €65 million
  • SME support measures for energy renovation: supporting SMEs to grow and create local employment with projects such as energy renovation of buildings or boosting energy efficiency for industry. €80 million

Denmark proposed amendments to the Plan, which were accepted by the Council in an implementing decision on 2 December 2024. Amendments include producing carbon rich soils through organic farming, organic transition of public kitchens; improving energy efficiency in public buildings and households and conducting a feasibility study for carbon capture and storage; and green tax reform including a higher carbon tax and tax deduction for investment in capacity costs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while increasing business operations.

Document Title: Law No. 33 of 9 April 2009
Family Title: Cleaner vehicle purchase incentives (Decree Law No. 5 of 2009)
Family Summary:
In February 2009, as part of measures aimed at supporting industrial sectors in crisis, the Council of Ministers launched a temporary incentive scheme for consumers to replace their old vehicles with new ones meeting certain environmental criteria.


Energy - demand-side policies: the scheme applies to cars, light commercial vehicles, as well as motorcycles and scooters. The incentives are provided in the form of a discount obtained by consumers directly from the dealers, who in turn receive this as a tax credit.


A bonus of EUR1,500 (USD1,882) is provided when a car more than nine years old and meeting Euro 0, 1 or 2 standards is exchanged for a new vehicle meeting Euro 4 or 5 standards and that emits a maximum of 130g CO2/km for diesel cars or 140g CO2/km for others. The exchanged vehicle must have been registered by December 1999.


This can be combined with a purchase incentive of EUR 1,500 should the new vehicle run on electricity, hydrogen or methane. Similar bonuses are provided for lightweight commercial vehicles, motorcycles and scooters.

Document Title: GB Energy Strategic Plan
Family Title: Great British Energy Act 2025
Family Summary:
Great British Energy (or GB Energy) is a publicly-owned and operationally independent company, headquartered in Aberdeen, supporting the delivery of the clean energy superpower mission of the United Kingdom. GB Energy will increase domestic clean energy production and public ownership of clean energy assets, build stronger UK supply chains, create jobs, and drive long-term growth of the local and community energy sector – ensuring the public benefits from the energy transition. Following from this objective, the company must secure that its articles of association contain a statement of its objects, which are restricted to facilitating, encouraging and participating in:

(a) the production, distribution, storage and supply of clean energy,

(b) the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from energy produced from fossil fuels,

(c) improvements in energy efficiency,

(d) measures for ensuring the security of the supply of energy, and

(e) measures for ensuring that slavery and human trafficking is not taking place in its business or supply chains,

(including through projects involving or benefitting local communities).

In December 2025, GB Energy published a Strategic Plan outlines a series of targets for 2030, including: the creation of an investment portfolio that aims to deliver 15GW in clear energy generation and mobilise £15billion of private finance by 2030; the support of over 1,000 local and community energy projects, with the objective of enhancing community ownership of projects; and supporting a just transition in areas that are historically dependent on oil and gas by funding projects that will create 10,000 new jobs, among other things.

Family Summary:
In February 2009, as part of measures aimed at supporting industrial sectors in crisis, the Council of Ministers launched a temporary incentive scheme for consumers to replace their old vehicles with new ones meeting certain environmental criteria.


Energy - demand-side policies: the scheme applies to cars, light commercial vehicles, as well as motorcycles and scooters. The incentives are provided in the form of a discount obtained by consumers directly from the dealers, who in turn receive this as a tax credit.


A bonus of EUR1,500 (USD1,882) is provided when a car more than nine years old and meeting Euro 0, 1 or 2 standards is exchanged for a new vehicle meeting Euro 4 or 5 standards and that emits a maximum of 130g CO2/km for diesel cars or 140g CO2/km for others. The exchanged vehicle must have been registered by December 1999.


This can be combined with a purchase incentive of EUR 1,500 should the new vehicle run on electricity, hydrogen or methane. Similar bonuses are provided for lightweight commercial vehicles, motorcycles and scooters.

Family Title: Directive (EU) 2018/2001 on the promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources, amended by Directive (EU) 2023/2413 (Renewable Energy Directive or RED)
Family Summary: This document establishes a common framework for the promotion of energy from renewable sources. It sets a binding Union target for the overall share of energy from renewable sources in the Union's gross final consumption of energy in 2030. It also lays down rules on financial support for electricity from renewable sources, on self-consumption of such electricity, on the use of energy from renewable sources in the heating and cooling sector and in the transport sector, on regional cooperation between Member States, and between Member States and third countries, on guarantees of origin, on administrative procedures and on information and training. It also establishes sustainability and greenhouse gas emissions saving criteria for biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels. Supplementing Regulation 2019/807 lays down the criteria for determining high indirect land-use change-risk feedstock for which a significant expansion of the production area into land with high carbon stock is observed and the certification of low indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels. As part of the EU's 'Fit for 55' package, a legislative package that aims to align the EU's climate, energy, land use, transport, and taxation policies with a GHG emissions reduction target of 55% by 2030 (compared with 1990 levels), this Directive has been reformed by the Directive (EU) 2023/2413 to set an overall binding renewable energy target of at least 42.5% in the EU's energy mix by 2030, while aiming for a target of 45%. Among the most important updates to the Directive are new provisions on bioenergy, targeted at preventing the degradation of carbon sinks and biodiversity loss associated with existing practices.

- provide a framework for and take effective response, adaptation and mitigation measures to facilitate the setting of specific objectives for sustainable development, security and energy efficiency.

- promote and manage sustainable development through climate change mitigation and adaptation activities; - set up financing mechanisms relating to climate change.

This Ordinance is also intended to supplement international instruments on the treatment of climate change.

Document Title: Water Policy Concept of the Slovak Republic to the year 2030
Family Title: Water Policy Concept of the Slovak Republic to the year 2030
Family Summary:
The implementation of the Water Policy Concept is based on the application of and compliance with the following principles:• Water as a vital environmental component and natural resourceWatercourses and the land under them are owned by the state. Water is essential for the functioning of society and ecosystems. Water and water-dependent ecosystems provide services and functions that a fundamental impact on the quality, quantity, availability and distribution of water. The use of water and ecosystems is only possible to the that their resilience is not impaired and that at least good ecological status of surface water bodies or good quantitative and chemical status of groundwater can be achieved/maintained.• Adapting to climate changeThe effects of climate change are manifested in all areas by an increase in the frequency of extreme meteorological and hydrological events (drought and water scarcity, floods), changes in the distribution of annual runoff, changes in groundwater recharge, landslides and soil erosion, changes in the stability of ecosystems and thus their ability to retain water and transform surface runoff, the spread of invasive species, etc. Adaptation measures and increasing the resilience of the landscape take precedence over addressing the consequences and negative impacts.• Water as a human rightAccess to water and sanitation is recognised as a fundamental human right and every member of society must have access to water in sufficient quantity and of adequate quality, including vulnerable and socially disadvantaged groups or individuals.

The objective is to have a resilient landscape capable of retaining water and mitigating the negative impacts of climate change, creating water resources of the required quality for sustainable consumption.

Document Title: The Natural Resources Conservation Authority (Air Quality) Regulations
Family Title: The Natural Resources Conservation Authority (Air Quality) Regulations
Family Summary:
• Regulates the emissions of particulates and substances deleterious to human health. This includes the licensing of premises and plants which produce such polluting substance; fees for discharge; and inspection.

    The Natural Resources Conservation Authority Act enabled the implementation of the Air Quality Regulations and these regulations legislate for the licensing, monitoring, and collection of fees for emissions. These emissions specifically include the term GHGs, and name these. The regulations seem to refer only to industrial sources, specifying facilities and stack emissions. The implication of these regulations is that industrial emissions will be licensed, monitored and have fees levied against them.

    Every owner of a major facility must apply for an air pollutant discharge licence and licensees must submit emissions reports for each calendar year. This report should contain estimates of the emissions for the year, based on the following details:Continuous emission monitoring data
  • Calculation of SO2 emissions based on fuel use and sulphur content data (combustion processes in which exhaust gases do not come in contact with products)
  • Most recent and representative stack monitoring measurements conducted in the previous five years and activity data for the year for which emissions are estimated
  • AP42 emission factor or equivalent methods and activity data for the year
  • AP42 emission factor or equivalent methods and plant capacity data
  • Mass balance (including fuel use data) based on the two previous years or the most recent representative year
  • Other approved methods supported by calculation and documentation

 
Further, the Regulations impose Discharge Fees on Licensees. Crucially, these fees are waived for emissions derived from the burning of renewable fuels, such as landfill gas and agricultural waste.

Where the regulations are not adhered to, sanctions may be applied to the licence holder. The management Authority (individual or body authorised under the regulations) may then:

  • Issue a control order
  • Impose administrative penalties
  • Suspend or revoke any licence
  • Refuse an application for renewal of any licence
  • Apply to the Supreme Court for an injunction to prohibit the operation of the facility or any source at the facility

 
The regulations also mandate the development of a National Emissions Inventory to track air quality, which should be made available to the public and reported to the House of Representatives at least once every three years.

Document Title: National Adaptation Plan - Energy
Family Title: Resolution S/N approving the National Adaptation Plan for Climate Change and Variability in the Energy Sector  (NAP-E)
Family Summary:
The NAP-E's main purpose is to improve the adaptability of the Uruguayan energy system, strengthen its resilience, and reduce its vulnerability to climate threats. This plan acknowledges the high levels of uncertainty associated with climate change, as well as the uncertainty inherent in technological evolution, and adopts an iterative, adaptive, and continuous learning approach. This approach will establish the necessary working processes to integrate climate change adaptation across all sectors, involving all key stakeholders, including the public sector, private sector, and academia.

The overall objective of the NAP-E is to reduce the climate vulnerability of the Uruguayan energy system to ensure it continues to fulfill its essential role of providing quality energy access to the population and contributing to the country’s sustainable development.

To achieve this objective, the NAP-E is structured around five lines of action to be implemented progressively, ensuring continuous and effective adaptation: Governance, Capacity strengthening and awareness, Information management and knowledge generation, Vulnerability reduction, and Monitoring, evaluation, and learning.

Document Title: Resolution 52/08, establishing the National Strategy for the Implementation of UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol
Family Title: Resolution 52/08, establishing the National Strategy for the Implementation of UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol
Family Summary:
Resolution 52/08 approved the National Implementation Strategy for the UNFCCC and the Kyoto Protocol. The Strategy requires that the government: (i) elaborates GHG inventories and reports about their impact on the environment and on public health; (ii) adopts programmes and projects to mitigate the effects of climate change; (iii) promotes technical/professional awareness; (iv) fosters international cooperation, particularly transfer of knowledge and experiences; (v) promotes the use of clean technologies; (vi) implement the Convention's and the Protocol's commitments; (vii) creates a structure and appropriate instruments for the management of Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms. Out of these activities, Angola submitted its Initial National Communication to UNFCCC in 2012. The communication contains the national GHG inventory. The GHG inventory comprises the following sectors: energy, industrial processes, agriculture, forestry, land use and waste. The government also established a Designated National Authority in 2009. Beyond that, education, awareness rising and investigation actions are being conducted. The Action Plan, which should have followed the approval of the strategy, was not prepared.
 
The National Strategy discusses the possibilities and opportunities that Angola has as a result of joining the Kyoto Protocol as well as the flexible mechanisms that can be used, especially in the case of Angola, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM).
 
 The Resolution sets the intervention framework for Angola in the legislative, technical and human domains. This framework should contribute to the stabilisation of GHG emissions and technological development of the country. The National Implementation Strategy comprises: generating reports and inventories about GHG emissions in Angola and their impact on the environment and public health; producing programmes and projects with measures to mitigate the effects of climate change; developing technical and professional training actions in areas related to climate change; fostering international co-operation within the context of climate change, particularly in terms of transfer of knowledge, experience and technology; and instituting the Designated National Authority (DNA) under the Ministry of the Environment as the entity responsible for coordinating inter-sectoral efforts for the implementation of UNFCCC in the country on the issues related to CDM. The DNA had its attributions defined through Government Order 2/10, being responsible for the execution of all CDM actions pertaining to the implementation of UNFCCC in the country.

Document Title: Report (White paper) on China's Policies and Actions to Address Climate Change
Family Title: Report (White paper) on China's Policies and Actions to Address Climate Change
Family Summary:
This white paper was prepared and published to report on China's progress on responding to climate change, share its practices and experiences, and enhance the understanding of the international community on its policies regarding climate change. It defines the government's long-term conceptual vision as aiming at promoting the construction of an ecological civilisation with high-quality development.


The paper reiterates that China's 14th Five-Year Plan outlines a binding indicator of "reducing carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 18% compared to 2020". It further states that in as of the end of 2019, China exceeded its 2020 target ahead of schedule and in 2020, China announced a new target: to peak its carbon dioxide emissions by 2030 and strive to achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. By 2030, China's carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP will decrease by more than 65% compared to 2005, and the proportion of non fossil fuels in primary energy consumption will reach about 25%. The forest stock will increase by 6 billion cubic meters compared to 2005, and the total installed capacity of wind and solar power will reach over 1.2 billion kilowatts. The proportion of non fossil fuels in primary energy consumption is increased by another five percentage points, and the target for increasing the installed capacity of non fossil fuels is increased. The forest storage volume is increased by another 1.5 billion cubic meters, with a clear goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2060.


The paper also notes that in 2021 China announced that it would no longer build new overseas coal-fired power projects.

Document Title: Philippine Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines
Family Title: Philippine Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines
Family Summary:
The Philippine Sustainable Finance Taxonomy Guidelines (SFTG) was developed under the auspices of the Financial Sector Forum (FSF) following the recommendations in the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap released by the Inter-agency Technical Working Group for Sustainable Finance (or the Green Force) in October 2021.

The SFTG serves as a tool to classify whether an economic activity is environmentally and socially sustainable and guides different stakeholders in making informed investment and financing decisions. The SFTG aims to direct, accelerate, and increase capital flows to economic activities that promote sustainability objectives. including reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and building climate resilience. It likewise promotes transparency and credibility by minimizing the risk of greenwashing and supports a just transition to a sustainable economy. Banks shall use the SFrG when extending credit. making investment decisions, or designing sustainable financial products and services, among others.

In issuing sustainable bonds, banks shall comply with the regulatory requirements articulated in the relevantsustainable bonds standards or guidelines issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). While the SEC Guidelines provide lists of eligible green and social project categories. the issuing bank may voluntarily apply the principles under the respective components of the SFTG to assess if such bond issuance is aligned with the Taxonomy. In addition. the considerations for the environmental objectives could provide additional guidance in assessing eligible green project and in determining substantial contribution to an environmental objective). There are decision trees and guiding questions provided for climate change adaptation and mitigation.

Document Title: Overview of the Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures: Cabinet Decision
Family Title: Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures
Family Summary:
The Plan for Global Warming Countermeasures was released by the Cabinet in order to promote global warming countermeasures comprehensively and strategically, based on the Paris agreement and Japan's INDC. The Plan is the legal and administration backbone for domestic implementation of Japanese emission reduction goals.

The plan initially defined a path to achieve a mid-term target of 26% greenhouse gas emission reduction by 2030 compared to 2013, clarifying cross-cutting policies and measures to be implemented, and also sets a long-term goal to pursue 80% reduction by 2050. In October 2021, the plan was updated to include a target of 46% greenhouse gas emission reduction by 2030, compared to 2013. It also sets a target for carbon neutrality by 2050. 

This plan lays down the foundations to the future progress of global warming countermeasures in Japan. Monitoring and evaluation mechanism inherent in the plan is a critical point for the steady implementation. The progress of actions will be reviewed every year, and the plan itself will be evaluated every three years.

Family Summary:

Document Title: Summary of the National Decarbonisation Plan
Family Title: Decarbonisation plan
Family Summary:
This plan sets out the government's strategy to decarbonise Costa Rica's economy until 2050. It differentiates between the initial phase (2018-2022), the inflection period (2022-2030), and the "massive deployment" (2031-2050).

The Plan is organised around ten focus areas:
1) Development of a mobility system base on safe, efficient and renewable public transport, and active and shared mobility schemes.
2) Transformation of the light duty vehicle fleet to a zero emissions one, nourished by energy that is renewable and not of fossil origin.
3) Promotion of a freight transport that adopts modalities, technologies and energy sources that emit zero or the lowest possible emissions.
4) Consolidation of the national electric system with the capacity, flexibility, intelligence, and resilience necessary to supply and manage renewable energy at competitive cost.
5) Development of buildings of different uses (commercial, residential, institutional) under high efficiency standards and low emission processes.
6) Modernization of the industrial sector through the application of electrical, efficient, and sustainable processes and technologies of low and zero emissions.
7) Development of an integrated waste management system based on the separation, reuse, revaluation, and final disposal of maximum efficiency and low greenhouse gas emissions.
8) Promotion of highly efficient agricultural food systems that generate low-carbon local consumption and export goods
9) Consolidation of an eco- competitive livestock model based on productive efficiency and reduction of greenhouse gases.
10) Consolidation of a model of management of rural, urban, and coastal territories that facilitates the protection of biodiversity, the increase and maintenance of forest cover and ecosystem services based on nature-based solutions.

Document Title: National Implementation Programme on Climate Adaptation (NUPKA)
Family Title: National Climate Adaptation Strategy (NAS)
Family Summary:
The National Climate Adaptation Strategy (NAS) was the Dutch answer to the call from the European Commission to all member states to create an adaptation strategy no later than 2017. The NAS included four diagrams (hotter, wetter, drier, and rising sea level) to visualise the effects of climate change on nine different sectors. The NAS 2016 was evaluated in 2022. In order to accelerate the implementation of the NAS 2016, a new report was published in 2023, titled “the National Implementation Programme on Climate Adaptation" in Dutch shortened to the "NUPKA". This document shows what measures have already been undertaken for the upcoming years, and which measurements are still necessary. It shows the implementation and speeding up of the NAS. In 2026 the new “NAS” will be published. 

The NUPKA (2023) states, for instance, that every development in the Netherlands from now on must take into account sea level rise, increasing heat, longer periods of drought, and more extreme rainfall. It also discusses that policies to make the Netherlands “climate proof” need to be more intelligent, intensive, and inclusive.

The NUPKA pays special attention to the following four domains:

  1. Water: protection against sea-level rise and flooding
  2. Agriculture, nature, and the environment: climate robust agriculture, resilient nature, and preparations for climate risks
  3. People and culture: heatproof cities, staying healthy in times of climate change, and protecting cultural heritage
  4. Living and working: climate-adaptive buildings and climate-proof living, resilient infrastructure, and resistant waterways

Document Title: Guide for the operation of the Peru carbon footprint tool (Guia para el funcionamiento de la herramiento huella de carbono Perú)
Family Title: Ministerial Resolution No. 185-2021-MINAM. Guide for the operation of the Peru Carbon Footprint tool (Resolución Ministerial Nº185-2021-MINAM. Guía para el funcionamiento de la herramienta Huella de Carbono Perú)
Family Summary: Peru's Ministerial Resolution N°185-2021-MINAM establishes the operational framework for the Peru Carbon Footprint (Huella de Carbono Perú) tool, a voluntary digital platform designed to promote greenhouse gas emissions management amongst public and private organisations. Created under Article 55 of the Climate Change Framework Law regulations, this free tool enables organisations to measure, verify, and reduce their GHG emissions whilst contributing to Peru's Nationally Determined Contributions implementation. The platform operates through a four-level system encompassing emissions measurement, third-party verification by accredited conformity assessment bodies, emissions reduction actions, and complementary measures, all aligned with international standards including ISO 14064-1:2020 and the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard.The tool functions as part of Peru's System for Monitoring Adaptation and Mitigation Measures, serving multiple climate objectives including sensitising organisations to emissions measurement through GHG inventory reporting, fostering emissions reductions that support NDC implementation, improving data quality for the national INFOCARBONO system, and establishing synergies between public and private climate initiatives.

Family Title: Multiannual Sectoral Strategic Plan for Transport and Communications 2024-2030 (Plan Estratégico Sectorial Multianual de Transporte y Comunicaciones 2024-2030)
Family Summary: The Multiannual Sectoral Strategic Plan (Plan Estratégico Sectorial Multianual "PESEM") 2024–2030 for Transport and Communications in Peru aims to align sectoral development with the National Strategic Development Plan (PEDN 2050) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It prioritises four strategic objectives: enhancing security and reliability of transport and communication systems; expanding access to quality services nationwide; improving competitiveness through sustainable and resilient infrastructure; and strengthening governance to ensure regulatory compliance. Document Title: Universal Energy Access Plan 2023-2027 (Plan de Acceso Universal a la Energía 2023-2027)
Family Title: Universal Energy Access Plan 2023-2027 (Plan de Acceso Universal de la Energía 2023-2027)
Family Summary: Peru’s Universal Energy Access Plan 2023-2027 charts a near-term pathway to deliver modern, reliable and affordable energy to all households (especially low-income, rural and peri-urban communities) while advancing the broader energy-transition goals set in the National Energy Policy 2010-2040. Centred on the principle of equity, the Plan commits to full coverage of electricity and clean fuels, backed by targeted subsidies, diversified financing (including the Fondo de Inclusión Social Energético) and six programme clusters: mass expansion of natural-gas networks; LPG access schemes; frontier electrification projects; rural-energy efficiency and productive-use initiatives; tariff-compensation mechanisms; and infrastructure to distribute clean cooking fuels. Priority is given to shifting households and transport from petroleum-based fuels to natural gas, electricity or other low-carbon alternatives, deploying the most efficient technologies available, and embedding safety and quality standards.

Collection Title(s): Environment and Planning Act of the Netherlands (Omgevingswet)
Collection Description(s):
The Environment and Planning Act (Omgevingswet) is a framework law that includes everything that is part of the “physical environment” (“leefomgeving”), and has come into force on January 1, 2024. The purpose of the Environment and Planning Act is to create a more coherent regulatory landscape for the physical environment by modernising, harmonising and combining laws into one single Act.

Overall, it (partially) repeals 26 laws and combines them into one single Act, including the Crisis & Recovery Act, the Environmental Management Act, and parts of the Water Act. Moreover, the Act reduces the previous 60 Orders in Council to 4 Orders in Council, and narrows down 75 ministerial regulations to one ‘Environment Regulation’.

Document Title: Italy's National Plan for Resilience and Recovery #NextGenerationItalia
Family Title: Italy's National Plan for Resilience and Recovery #NextGenerationItalia
Family Summary:
To benefit from the support of the Recovery and Resilience Facility set up by the EU in the aftermath of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis, Member States submit their recovery and resilience plans to the European Commission. Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient. The Commission validates the plan after which it effectively enters in force and EU subsidies can start flowing towards the member state.

37% of the plan’s total allocation is assessed to be directed towards reforms and investments supports climate objectives. Notable investments include the following:

  • Sustainable mobility: integrate more regions into the high-speed rail network and complete the rail freight corridors; boost sustainable local transport through the extension of cycle lanes, metros, tramways and zero- emission buses, including the construction of electric charging stations across the country and hydrogen refuelling points for road and rail transport. €32.1 billion
  • Energy efficiency in residential buildings: financing large-scale renovation of residential buildings to make them more energy efficient. €12.1 billion The plan supports interventions for the improvement of energy efficiency of residential buildings by which beneficiaries may benefit from a tax rebate over the next five years for the amounts spent, provided that the energy savings of those interventions are higher than 30%. By the end of 2025, building renovation interventions will be completed for at least 32 million square meters.
  • Renewable energy and circular economy: developing the production and incentivising the use of renewable energies including green hydrogen as well as increasing recycling, reducing landfill waste and improving water management. €11.2 billion

Document Title: Final Rule - Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Establishing the Allowance Allocation and Trading Program under the AIM Act
Family Title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021
Family Summary: This 2,000 pages-long document implements a major government funding scheme and also includes economic stimulus provisions to respond to the coronavirus pandemic. It notably contains the Energy Act 2020.The document contains numerous climate-related clauses. It notably encourages GHG emissions reductions and promotes renewables. It contains a part on carbon use and sets processes to estimate the economic, climate, and environmental impacts of any well-integrated national carbon dioxide pipeline system. It mandates the Climate Security Advisory Council to develop a study on advisory council model for strategic or transnational threats.The American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020 was enacted as section 103 in Division S of this document (page 1074 onward). The AIM Act directs EPA to address HFCs by providing new authorities in three main areas: to phase down the production and consumption of listed HFCs, manage these HFCs and their substitutes, and facilitate the transition to next-generation technologies. On September 23rd, 2021, the EPA administrator signed a notice to allow for the publication of the final rule for a 15-year phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). The rule sets the HFC production and consumption baseline levels from which reductions will be made, establishes an initial methodology for allocating and trading HFC allowances for 2022 and 2023, and creates a robust, agile, and innovative compliance and enforcement system. The EPA estimates that it will avoid cumulative emissions of 4,560 million metric tons of exchange value equivalent of HFCs in the United States with a present value of cumulative net benefits of $272.7 billion, from 2022 to 2050.

Document Title: The Environment Decree of the Netherlands (Omgevingsbesluit)
Family Title: The Environment Decree of the Netherlands (Omgevingsbesluit)
Family Summary:
The Environment Decree of the Netherlands (Omgevingsbesluit) contains rules on who is the competent authority for environmental permits, which procedure applies, enforcement and implementation, and how environmental impact assessment takes place. It also contains the Digital System for the Environment Act (DSO). Overall this Decree applies to all parties active in the physical environment - citizens, businesses, and government. The Decree also applies in the exclusive economic zone (the Dutch part of the North Sea). 

It contains rules on the content and monitoring of Environmental Impact Assessment (Chapter 11) for plans, projects, and programmes, including a description of “the impact of the project on the climate and the vulnerability of the project to climate change” (11.18 f). The Decree also includes rules regarding transboundary environmental effects (11.3), and details around the advisory bodies and advisors for environmental assessment. Furthermore, Chapter 9 contains rules concerning damage.
Collection Title(s): Environment and Planning Act of the Netherlands (Omgevingswet)
Collection Description(s):
The Environment and Planning Act (Omgevingswet) is a framework law that includes everything that is part of the “physical environment” (“leefomgeving”), and has come into force on January 1, 2024. The purpose of the Environment and Planning Act is to create a more coherent regulatory landscape for the physical environment by modernising, harmonising and combining laws into one single Act.

Overall, it (partially) repeals 26 laws and combines them into one single Act, including the Crisis & Recovery Act, the Environmental Management Act, and parts of the Water Act. Moreover, the Act reduces the previous 60 Orders in Council to 4 Orders in Council, and narrows down 75 ministerial regulations to one ‘Environment Regulation’.

Document Title: Amendment, published in Bulletin of Acts, Orders, and Decrees
Family Title: The Environment Buildings Decree of the Netherlands  (Besluit bouwwerken leefomgeving, Bbl)
Family Summary:
The Environment Buildings Decree of the Netherlands (Besluit bouwwerken leefomgeving, Bbl) contains rules on construction, demolition,and the use and maintenance of buildings, in order to enhance the safety, health, sustainability, and operability of buildings. Together with the Environmental Activities Decree (Bal) this Decree updates the systematic approach to enhance energy efficiency by companies and institutions. One example of improving the sustainability of the built environment is the policy that all office buildings in the Netherlands require an energy label of C or better from 1 January 2023. 

The Decree was first published in 2018, and amended later in 2023 in order to “make energy use more sustainable” as is stated to be “an important means to achieve the government’s emission reduction targets”. In the amendment, the following changes were made

  • The Energy Saving Obligation is broadened to an obligation to take measures to make energy use more sustainably. This means measures for on-site renewable energy production, and switching energy sources to one with lower carbon emissions will become mandatory if they have a payback period of no more than five years
  • The target group for the Energy Saving Obligation is expanded, this is done through declaring the energy-saving obligation applicable to environmentally harmful activities that require a permit, and by removing the exception in certain cases
  • Updates the information obligation to report on sustainable energy measures

Document Title: Energy Security Strategy of the Slovak Republic, Resolution of the Government No. 732/2008 Coll.
Family Title: Energy Security Strategy of the Slovak Republic, Resolution of the Government No. 732/2008 Coll.
Family Summary:
The Energy Security Strategy assesses the current energy situation of the Slovak Republic and proposes measures and legislation to be adopted to increase energy security of the country.

The key objective of the Energy Security Strategy is to guarantee competitiveness of the energy sector, to provide secure, reliable and efficient supply of all forms of energy at affordable prices with regard to consumer protection, the environment, sustainable development, security of supply and technical security.

The Strategy aims at ensuring self-sufficiency in electricity production, an optimal pricing policy, pro-export ability, strengthening the position of Slovakia as a transit country in the electricity, gas and oil markets, and guarantee reliable supply of thermal energy and other energy carriers. The Strategy also presents different possible scenarios of the energy security development with regard to coal, oil, natural gas, heat, electricity and renewables supply, and energy efficiency. It proposes measures for securing supply of each resource.

Family Title: National Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting Regulations, 2016
Family Summary: This document amends the National Environmental Management Air Quality Act. The purpose of the National Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reporting Regulations is to introduce a single national reporting system for the transparent reporting of greenhouse gas emissions, which will be used to maintain a National Greenhouse Gas Inventory, allow South Africa to meet its UNFCCC reporting obligations and to inform the formulation and implementation of legislation and policy. The emission sources and data providers who are covered by the Regulations are set out in Annexure 1 and Regulation 4. The Regulations also set out the reporting requirements, calculation methodology, verification procedure (to be carried out by the National Inventory Unit) and penalties (which include fines and imprisonment).The declaration of 21 July, 2017 officially recognises greenhouse gases as priority air pollutants.

Document Title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1405 amending Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126 as regards the total quantities of cancelled EU ETS allowances that may be taken into account for certain Member States’ compliance under Regulation (EU) 2018/842
Family Title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126 on setting out the annual emission allocations of the Member States for the period from 2021 to 2030 pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2018/842
Family Summary:
Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2020/2126, adopted on 16 December 2020, establishes the annual greenhouse gas emission allocations (AEAs) for each EU Member State for the period 2021–2030 under the Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR). It defines the 2005 baseline emissions for every Member State and specifies the annual emission limits each country must respect throughout the decade. The Decision also sets out the total quantities that can be used for compliance through flexibility mechanisms, such as limited use of ETS allowances or land-use credits. Three annexes provide detailed data: Annex I lists the 2005 baseline emissions, Annex II gives the annual emission allocations for each year from 2021 to 2030, and Annex III sets out the total quantities available under flexibility provisions.

Since its adoption, the Decision has been amended several times to update the data and reflect changes in EU climate policy. Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1319 revised the AEAs for 2023–2030 to align with the higher climate ambition introduced by the revised Effort Sharing Regulation. Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/1884 introduced further updates and corrections to the national allocations, ensuring consistency with the most recent emissions data. Finally, Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1405 made additional adjustments, likely to incorporate updated figures or methodological improvements. Together, these amendments ensure that Member States’ emission limits remain accurate and in line with the evolving EU legislative framework and climate targets.
Collection Description(s): he Effort Sharing Regulation (ESR) is an EU law that sets binding annual greenhouse gas emission targets for each member state in sectors not covered by the EU Emissions Trading System — like transport, buildings, agriculture, and waste. Its goal is to ensure a fair contribution from all countries toward the EU’s overall climate targets.

Document Title: White Paper on Transport Policy 2021
Family Title: White Paper on Transport Policy 2021
Family Summary:
This White Paper is a policy document aimed at providing a transport system that is environmentally benign and supports economic and environmental sustainability and inclusive growth. This Paper was published after a review of the White Paper on National Transport Policy of 1996. One of the environmental considerations is to reduce the impact of transport on climate change by promoting low-carbon modes of transport in the design of transportation systems.

The White Paper sets out the policy of planning for the provision of transport infrastructure within an integrated environmental management approach which will include, inter alia, the performance of environmental impact assessments. Considerations will include environmental impacts, energy conservation, the transport of dangerous materials and the conservation of scarce infrastructure construction materials. In addition, low-carbon modes of transportation should be prioritised in the design of transportation systems. Other policy measures include fuel efficiency; lower energy intensity; reduction of negative impact on biodiversity and air quality; and the mixed-use developments to provide places of work close to home.

Document Title: Pact for Ecological Transformation
Family Title: Pact for Ecological Transformation between the three branches of the Brazilian State
Family Summary:
The Pact for Ecological Transformation is a commitment signed by the Executive, Legislative and Judicial branches to act in a harmonious and integrated manner to promote ecological transformation through legislative, administrative and judicial measures.

Its main commitments are:

  • The Legislative Branch will prioritise bills related to the pact's themes, such as the approval of the legal framework for the carbon market, offshore wind energy production and biofuels;
  • The Judiciary will adopt measures to speed up judicial demands involving environmental, land and climate issues, including the definition of targets and protocols by the National Council of Justice (CNJ);
  • The executive branch will expand funding and reduce the cost of credit for sustainable sectors, projects and practices;
  • The executive branch and the judiciary will jointly integrate real estate, environmental, cadastral and tax databases, with georeferenced data, to guarantee legal certainty about the ownership of public and private land in the country, as well as unlock investment.
  • The Legislative, Executive and Judicial branches will adopt management measures to reduce the direct impacts of their activities on the environment, such as sustainable bidding, reducing demand for natural resources, energy efficiency and proper waste disposal.

Document Title: Environmental Policy Guidelines for 2021-2027

They have been developed in accordance with the priorities set out in the Latvia 2030, Latvian NDP for 2021-2027 and the strategic objectives of the European Green Course and provide for:

  • achieving the 2030 greenhouse gas reduction target and achieve climate neutrality by 2050;
  • improving adaptability, strengthening resilience and reducing vulnerability to climate change;
  • making progress towards a renewable growth model by decoupling economic growth from resource use and environmental depletion and acceleration of the transition to a circular economy;
  • aiming for zero pollution in the environment free of toxic substances, including air, water and soil, and thus also protecting the health and well-being of Europeans;
  • protecting, preserving and restoring biodiversity and increasing natural capital, in particular air, water, soil, and forest, freshwater, wetland and marine ecosystems; and
  • promoting environmental sustainability and reducing environmental and climate pressures related to production and consumption, in the fields of energy, industrial development, buildings and infrastructure, mobility and food systems.

Family Title: Action Plan to Accelerate Renewables Projects in Tunisia
Family Summary: The Action Plan to Accelerate Renewables Projects in Tunisia is a subsidiary of the 2015 Solar Plan, and aims to facilitate its implementation, reaffirming its goals for 2020 and 2030, and extending ambitions further towards 2050. The action plan sets out goals for government wind and solar energy supply concessions, acquisition of public and private finance, review and revision of authorisation requirements, fast-tracked access for small renewable projects, revision of metering/billing systems, identification of land constraints, creation of an independent regulator and help-desk, and better research systems to forecast supply and demand.

Document Title: National Climate Finance Strategy of Belize 2021-2026
Family Title: National Climate Finance Strategy of Belize 2021-2026
Family Summary: The National Climate Finance Strategy of Belize 2021-2026 notes that the ambition level of the country's NDCs is highly dependent on access to adequate finance, and as such the strategy aims to enhance climate financing for adaptation and mitigation in the short to medium term. As core strategic directions it aims to prioritise climate adaptation, leverage international private and public finance, promote domestic private climate finance, enhance financing based on carbon assets, climate-proof development projects across the economy, build a co-ordinated risk financing mechanism, and explore non-conventional climate finance strategies.

Document Title: Strategic Plan for the Common Agricultural Policy for 2023-2027 – summary version 6.1
Family Title: Poland's CAP Strategic Plan (2023-2027)
Family Summary: Poland’s CAP Strategic Plan (Plan strategiczny WPR 2023-2027) is the country’s national implementation of the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy for 2023-27, approved by the European Commission on 31 August 2022. It aims to support sustainable development of Polish farms and rural areas, boosting farm income, competitiveness, innovation and risk management, while placing strong emphasis on environmental and climate protection, including measures to improve water management, reduce greenhouse gas and ammonia emissions, protect soil, air and biodiversity, and promote sustainable energy and resource use. The plan also fosters social and economic activation in rural areas and the spread of innovation and digital solutions throughout agriculture.

Document Title: Regulation on the Management of Industrial Emissions
Family Title: Regulation on the Management of Industrial Emissions
Family Summary: The purpose of this Regulation is to regulate the administrative and technical procedures and principles for green transformation, circular economy and decarbonisation in industry to prevent and minimize the formation of industrial emissions and waste accumulation that cause air, water, soil, noise and odour pollution, and to use resources efficiently, with a control approach, in order to integrate the zero pollution target for the holistic protection of the environment and human health.

Document Title: National Strategy for the Development of Green Hydrogen and its Derivatives in Tunisia, 2024
Family Title: National Strategy for the Development of Green Hydrogen and its Derivatives in Tunisia, 2024
Family Summary: The National Strategy for the Development of Green Hydrogen and its Derivatives in Tunisia (2024) aims to promote a green hydrogen industry, beginning with the domestic development of green ammonia for the fertiliser sector. The strategy aims to expand to hydrogen exports and green synthetic fuels in the longer term, exporting 6.3 megatonnes of hydrogen to the EU by 2050.

Document Title: National Development Concept 2050
Family Title: National Development Concept 2050
Family Summary: The National Development Concept 2050 is Poland’s first long-term strategic vision, setting out the country’s development directions through the middle of the 21st century. It uses foresight, forecasting, and scenario analysis to identify potential development pathways and key societal, economic, and environmental challenges. This policy shifts the economic paradigm by treating the natural environment not as an infinite resource, but as a critical form of capital that must be preserved for "generational justice". A primary focus of the concept is a comprehensive energy transformation, which mandates a transition away from fossil fuels toward a zero-emission system powered by renewables and nuclear energy. Beyond power generation, the strategy emphasizes the adoption of a circular economy and a "moderate" consumption model to drastically reduce Poland's overall ecological footprint. To address the physical realities of a warming world, the document prioritizes building national resilience through blue-green infrastructure designed to mitigate the risks of extreme weather events like droughts and floods. Furthermore, it integrates climate action into spatial planning and education, aiming to foster a society that is both environmentally sensitive and structurally prepared for the challenges of the mid-21st century.This Concept was adopted by y the Council of Ministers on 25 July 2025.

Document Title: Tunisian Solar Plan
Family Title: Tunisian Solar Plan
Family Summary: The Tunisian Solar Plan identifies solar energy as a major opportunity for energy development and climate change mitigation, and sets an agenda for the long term expansion of the sector, with an emphasis on setting targets for 2030. By 2030, It aims to achieve a 3815 MW solar capacity, representing a 35% share of the electricity supply. The plan provides a roadmap for its implementation, including the establishment of an independent energy regulator, robust public information, technical training programs, and research/development support on smart grids and forecasting to ensure grid efficient grid integration.

Document Title: Energy Strategy Synthesis for 2035
Family Title: Energy Strategy Synthesis for 2035
Family Summary: The Energy Strategy Synthesis for 2035 sets a long term framework for the development of the energy sector in Tunisia. It aims to strengthen energy security, reduce fossil fuel imports, combat energy poverty, and contribute to carbon neutrality by 2050. The strategy promotes investment in renewables, electrification of transport and alternative fuels such as green hydrogen. It aims for a renewable energy capacity of 8350MW by 2035.

Document Title: Act of 20 July 2017 - Water Law (Consolidated text)
Family Title: Act of 20 July 2017 - Water Law
Family Summary: The Polish Water Law establishes an integrated framework for managing water resources with strong relevance for climate adaptation, energy security, and disaster risk management. It explicitly addresses climate-related pressures by prioritising protection against floods and droughts, introducing risk-based planning, flood hazard and risk mapping, and the use of retention, polders, and coastal protection infrastructure to reduce climate-driven extremes. The Act supports the energy sector, particularly hydropower and water-dependent infrastructure, by regulating water use, permitting, and the operation of water and flood-control structures while balancing these activities with ecological objectives. Through river-basin planning, hydrological and meteorological monitoring, and coordination with EU climate and environmental directives, the law strengthens Poland’s resilience to climate change, reduces vulnerability to water-related disasters, and ensures that energy development and water management contribute to long-term environmental and societal safety. The last amendment provided by the Act (Dz.U. 2025 poz. 1535) modernises and expands Poland’s legal framework for offshore wind and other renewables.

Document Title: Polish Nuclear Power Programme
Family Title: Polish Nuclear Power Programme
Family Summary:
The programme presents the scope and structure of the organization of activities to be undertaken in order to:

  • implement nuclear energy,
  • ensure the safe and effective operation of nuclear power facilities,
  • ensure decommissioning of nuclear power facilities after the end of their operational lifetime,
  • ensure the safety of spent fuel and radioactive waste management.
  • The Program implementation schedule has been set out for the years 2020-2043;

Document Title: Strategy of the National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management (NFOŚiGW) for 2025–2028
Family Title: Strategy of the National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management (NFOŚiGW) for 2025–2028
Family Summary:
The Strategy of the National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management (NFOŚiGW) for 2025–2028 is a strategic roadmap designed to reinforce the Fund's role as a leader in financing Poland's green transition. The main goal is to drive the green transition and support low-emission transformation, sustainable development, and environmental improvement in Poland through effective pro-environmental initiatives.

The document divides environmental priorities into two categories (i) sectoral: Energy transformation, air quality improvement, circular economy (waste and water management), and biodiversity protection and (ii) horizontal: Climate change adaptation, environmental monitoring, expert research, ecological education, and innovation.

All in all, the strategy is highly climate-centric, aligning with the EU Green Deal and Poland's national energy policies.

The strategy was adopted by Resolution 103/2024 on June 27, 2024.

Document Title: Strategy for Sustainable Transport Development 2030
Family Title: Strategy for Sustainable Transport Development 2030
Family Summary:
The main goal of the national transport policy outlined in the strategy is to increase the country's transport accessibility, improve the safety of road users, and enhance the efficiency of the transport sector by creating a coherent, sustainable, innovative, and user-friendly transport system at the national, European, and global levels. Achieving this goal will foster favorable conditions for the country's stable economic development.

The document also indicates modern solutions that facilitate the functioning of the entire transport sector, reducing its negative impact on the environment and climate, so as to create a sustainable transport system for the country by 2030.The strategy was adopted by Resolution 105/2019 on 24 September 2019.

Document Title: Resolution 123/2019 adopting the Strategy for Sustainable Rural, Agricultural and Fisheries Development 2030
Family Title: Strategy for Sustainable Rural, Agricultural and Fisheries Development 2030
Family Summary: The Strategy for Sustainable Development of Rural Areas, Agriculture and Fisheries 2030 (SZRWRiR 2030) aims to ensure food security, increase the economic value added from agriculture, and sustainably raise incomes of rural residents while reducing economic, social and territorial disparities and improving the natural environment. The strategy pursues three complementary objectives: strengthening food security and resilience to crises, improving quality of life and environmental conditions, and developing entrepreneurship and non-agricultural employment. It sets out integrated directions of intervention and actions that are financed from national and EU funds, with a strong emphasis on modernisation, innovation, environmental sustainability and increasing sector resilience to climate change.The strategy was adopted by Resolution 123/2019 on 15 October 2019.

Document Title: Strategy for Responsible Development for the period up to 2020 (including the perspective up to 2030)
Family Title: Strategy for Responsible Development for the period up to 2020 (including the perspective up to 2030)
Family Summary: The Strategy for Responsible Development until 2020 (with a 2030 outlook) – SOR – was adopted by the Council of Ministers on February 14, 2017. It was designed as a medium-term blueprint to transition Poland from a growth model reliant on low labor costs to one fueled by innovation and institutional efficiency. From a climate perspective, the SOR integrates environmental responsibility into economic modernization by promoting a circular economy and spearheading low-emission initiatives, such as the large-scale development of electromobility and the "Clean Air" program. It also addresses climate-related vulnerabilities by mandating investments in blue-green infrastructure to manage water scarcity and extreme weather risks. Ultimately, while the SOR provides the immediate operational framework for these transitions, it now serves as a foundational bridge toward the much longer-term goal of total climate neutrality envisioned for 2050.

Document Title: Resolution 180/2023
Family Title: National Shipping Programme until 2030
Family Summary: The National Shipping Programme until 2030 is aimed at increasing the role of inland waterway transport nationally and locally. It prioritises modernising hydrotechnical infrastructure on key river corridors (Odra and Wisła) to support efficient waterborne freight, which can shift cargo from road to lower-emission transport, and includes measures aimed at reducing the emissions intensity of inland vessels and promoting improved traffic management systems that can cut fuel use and pollution.

Document Title: National Regional Development Strategy
Family Title: National Regional Development Strategy
Family Summary: The National Regional Development Strategy (KSRR 2030 - in Polish) is Poland’s key strategic document guiding regional policy through 2030, built around a model of socially sensitive and territorially balanced development that responds to regional disparities and supports inclusive growth. It aims to increase national cohesion by leveraging internal territorial potentials, reducing socio‑economic inequalities between regions (including rural/urban divides), and strengthening the competitive advantages of all areas. To achieve this, the strategy sets three core objectives: reducing development disparities in social, economic, environmental and spatial dimensions; enhancing regional competitive strengths; and improving governance and implementation of territorially focused policies.

Document Title: Resolution No. 144/2023 - National Railway Programme until 2030 (with a perspective until 2032)
Family Title: Resolution No. 144/2023 - National Railway Programme until 2030 (with a perspective until 2032)
Family Summary: The National Railway Programme (KPK) is a multi-year program encompassing investments in railway lines, co-financed by the Minister of Transport. The document specifies the amount and sources of funding (including EU and national funds) and provides the basis for ensuring investment financing in accordance with the Public Finance Act. As a result of the update adopted by the Council of Ministers on August 16, 2023, the program's name was changed to the National Railway Program until 2030 (with an outlook to 2032). This aligns the program's duration with the European Union's financial framework for 2021-2027, with some projects planned for implementation by 2032.

Document Title: Resolution No. 33/2015 of the Council of Ministers on the Maritime Policy of the Republic of Poland until 2020 (with a perspective until 2030)
Family Title: Resolution No. 33/2015 of the Council of Ministers on the Maritime Policy of the Republic of Poland until 2020 (with a perspective until 2030)
Family Summary: The Maritime Policy of the Republic of Poland until 2020 (with a perspective to 2030) integrates environmental protection and climate action into the strategic development of the maritime sector. A central focus is the promotion of maritime transport as one of the most eco-friendly ways to move cargo, with specific goals to develop "green ships" featuring ecological propulsion systems. The policy emphasizes the expansion of offshore renewable energy, specifically targeting the development of offshore wind farms, wave energy, and current power to diversify the national energy mix. For instance, it set an objective for offshore wind farms to reach a capacity of 500 MW by 2020. To address the physical impacts of climate change, the policy outlines rigorous coastal protection measures, including the stabilization of the coastline and the enhancement of flood defense systems for coastal areas.

Document Title: Long-term building renovation strategy
Family Title: Long-term building renovation strategy
Family Summary: Poland’s Długoterminowa strategia renowacji budynków (Long-Term Building Renovation Strategy) is a strategy adopted by the Council of Ministers in February 2022 that sets out how to deeply renovate the country’s building stock up to 2050 to improve energy efficiency, cut greenhouse gas emissions and reduce air pollution. It aims to carry out about 7.5 million energy-efficiency renovations (including 4.7 million deep renovations) by mid-century, support the transition to climate-neutral buildings, accelerate replacement of high-emission heating sources, and integrate national and EU financial and legislative support to make renovations cost-effective and socially equitable while boosting jobs and economic benefits.

Document Title: Framework Action Plan for Organic Food and Farming (2021-2030)
Family Title: Framework Action Plan for Organic Food and Farming (2021-2030)
Family Summary: The Framework Action Plan for Organic Food and Farming in Poland for 2021-2030 has been updated to align with the European Union's "Farm to Fork" strategy. As of recent updates in 2024-2025, Poland’s Framework Action Plan for Organic Food and Farming in Poland for 2021–2030 aims to develop organic production, including the development of the organic products market in Poland and to allocate at least 7% of the agricultural area covered by the organic production system by 2030.This goal means doubling the area of ​​agricultural land covered by this system by 2030 compared to 2019 and striving to reach over one million hectares of this area.

Document Title: Energy for Rural Areas Priority Programme (Energia dla wsi)
Family Title: Energy for Rural Areas Priority Programme
Family Summary:
The "Energy for Rural Areas" (Polish: Energia dla wsi) priority programme is a major initiative launched by the Polish government, funded through the EU Modernisation Fund, to accelerate the deployment of renewable energy sources (RES) in rural and rural-urban municipalities.

The program funds the construction of:

  • Photovoltaic (PV) installations.
  • Wind installations.
  • Hydropower plants.
  • Agricultural biogas plants.
  • Integrated energy storage facilities.

The first call of applications happened in 2023 and the second round in 2025.

Document Title: Comprehensive program for counteracting forest dieback processes in Poland and mitigation measures in the perspective of 2030
Family Title: Comprehensive program for counteracting forest dieback processes in Poland and mitigation measures in the perspective of 2030
Family Summary: The Comprehensive Programme to Counter Forest Dieback in Poland up to 2030 (KPPPZL 2030) adopted by Decision 201 of the Director General of the State Forest addresses the increasing problem of forest dieback in Poland driven by climate change, drought, pests and habitat degradation, with a focus on preventing large-scale tree mortality and preserving healthy forest ecosystems. It sets out coordinated management, protection and adaptation measures to increase forest resilience, limit tree mortality, protect biodiversity and maintain forests’ ecological and climate functions, including carbon sequestration and water regulation.

Document Title: Agroenergy Programme (Agroenergia)
Family Title: Agroenergy Programme (Agroenergia)
Family Summary:
The aim of the program is to increase energy production from renewable sources in the agricultural sector. The program will be implemented until 2027.The Agroenergia program consists of two parts:

  • Micro-installations, heat pumps and accompanying energy storage - Types of subsidized projects: photovoltaic installations, wind installations and heat pumps with an installed capacity above 10 kW and not exceeding 50 kW, including hybrid installations and accompanying electricity storage facilities.
  • Agricultural biogas plants and small hydropower plants - Types of subsidized projects: agricultural biogas plants with an accompanying agricultural biogas production installation and hydroelectric power plants with a capacity of no more than 500 kW with accompanying energy storage facilities.

Document Title: Biofuels Act - No. 1676 of 30/12/2024 (latest amendment)
Family Title: Act on Sustainable Biofuels and on the Reduction of Greenhouse Gases (Biofuels Act)
Family Summary:
The purpose of the Act is to promote the use of sustainable biofuels for land transport and to reduce cradle-to-grave greenhouse gas emissions from transport in order to contribute to the fulfillment of Denmark's international climate commitments. The Act sets mandatory levels of biofuels use for companies and is regularly amended to update these levels.The 2016 amendment introduces requirements for the use of 0.9 per cent of advanced biofuels in land transport fuels, amends the definition of which companies are covered by the law, and authorises to establish rules for compliance with MRV regulation to promote CO2 emissions reduction from maritime transport and rules on access to ships. 2019 and 2020 updates are to the list of advanced biofuels; and duty of companies to ensure biofuels make up at least 7.6% of company’s total annual sale of fuels (following European counting rules).

The latest amendment of 30 December 2024 expands coverage of the Act to the aviation sector and stipulates that the Minister may lay down rules on penalties for fines for violations of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation. The Minister for Climate, Energy and Utilities may also lay down rules on payments, including fees or other payments, to cover the authorities' costs of administration and supervision of compliance with the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation and of rules issued pursuant to this Act, the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation.

Document Title: RFTO Compliance Guidance
Family Title: Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation (RTFO) Scheme
Family Summary:
The RTFO delivers greenhouse gas (GHG) emission savings by encouraging the supply of renewable fuels for use in UK transport. Under the RTFO, suppliers of relevant transport fuel (petrol, diesel, gas oil or renewable fuel) in the UK must meet an annual obligation using tradeable certificates which are awarded for the supply of sustainable renewable fuel. The RTFO is administered by a team within the Department for Transport (DfT) called the Low Carbon Fuels (LCF) Delivery Unit.

Suppliers of relevant fuel totalling 450,000 litres or more for use in a relevant transport mode during an obligation period must register with the LCF Delivery Unit and may be subject to an obligation. The relevant transport modes are:

  • road vehicles;
  • non-road transports – including non-road mobile machinery (NRMM); and
  • maritime, if the fuel used is a renewable fuel of non-biological origin (RFNBO).

The obligation has 2 elements – the ‘main obligation’ and the ‘development fuel target’. The obligation is calculated by multiplying the obligated amount (the total fossil and unsustainable renewable fuel supplied) by the obligation percentage for that period. For 2025, this percentage is 14.054% for the main obligation and 1.619% for the development fuel target.

Obligated suppliers can meet their obligation by redeeming Renewable Transport Fuel Certificates (RTFCs) or by paying a fixed sum for each litre of fuel for which they wish to ‘buy-out’ of their obligation. An obligated supplier can obtain RTFCs either by supplying renewable fuels, or by buying them from renewable fuel suppliers. DfT sets the buy-out priceand the market determines certificate prices based on supply and demand.
