Document Title: Presidential Decree 5681 on Regulatory Impact Analysis
Family Title: Presidential Decree 5681 on Regulatory Impact Analysis
Family Summary: Presidential decree on the Procedures and Principles for the Implementation of Regulatory Impact Analysis was published in the Official Gazette on 4 June 2022, under issue number 31856, outlined the mandatory guidelines for conducting regulatory impact assessments (RIAs) and strategic environmental assessments (SEAs). These critical tools ensure that regulatory and non-regulatory proposals are developed with a clear understanding of their potential impacts. Türkiye mandated the preparation of RIAs to systematise the evaluation of potential effects of proposed regulations, including climate change-related ones.

Family Title: 2025 Cabinet decision approving National Building Code recommendations

Document Title: National Action Plan for Climate Change and Natural Disaster Risks (Decree no.362)
Family Title: National Action Plan for Climate Change and Natural Disaster Risks (Decree no.362)
Family Summary: The National Action Plan for Climate Change and Natural Disaster Risks (Decree no.362) promotes a wide range of actions across sectors to reduce Uzbekistan's vulnerability to natural disasters, including those induced by climate change. It acknowledges particular climate-driven risk from extreme rainfall events, forest fires and physical vulnerability of dams and reservoirs. The action plan aims to build institutional capacity for proactive measures and response, educate the general population, attract investment and better predict and monitor climate risks. It promotes intervention through a range of sectors including healthcare, buildings, agriculture, meteorology, government ministries and financial institutions.

Document Title: Decree UP-106 On the Establishment of The Climate Council Under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Family Title: Decree UP-106 On the Establishment of The Climate Council Under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Family Summary: Decree UP-106 establishes a national climate council as the highest advisory body to the president on climate adaptation and mitigation, to better co-ordinate and unify national climate policy. The decree and formation of the council initiates the process of developing a national climate mitigation and adaptation strategy. Aside from strategic and legislative efforts, the decree also places emphasis on the expansion and integration of carbon trading systems nationally.

Document Title: Decree PP-233 On Measures to Create a Climate-Resilient Agro-Ecosystem and Increase the Resilience of Agricultural Producers to the Risks Associated with Climate Change
Family Title: Decree PP-233 On Measures to Create a Climate-Resilient Agro-Ecosystem and Increase the Resilience of Agricultural Producers to the Risks Associated with Climate Change
Family Summary: Decree PP-233 implements a package of national and international funding for agricultural climate adaptation measures, setting priorities, responsibilities and subsequent action. Measures include ecosystem restoration, urban green space expansion, environmental early warning systems, anti-desertification afforestation, low-till agriculture implementation, climate action verification systems, on-site adaptation training seminars for land managers, and substantial media coverage of these issues and projects.

Document Title: Resolution PP-4896 On Measures to Further Improve the Activities of the Hydrometeorological Service Center of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Family Title: Resolution PP-4896 On Measures to Further Improve the Activities of the Hydrometeorological Service Center of the Republic of Uzbekistan
Family Summary: Resolution PP-4896 aims to consolidate, restructure and guide the development of the national hydrometeorological service centre (Uzhydromet), to improve the production and availability of climatic and hydrological data nationally. It enshrines the necessity of funding ongoing climate change research, and the integration of this service with national climate adaptation efforts. It also promotes the public dissemination and awareness of climate change data, through publications, seminars, internships and other means. The resolution underscores the importance of fulfilling international obligations on climate reporting and action, and envisages participation of national climate research authorities in the development of international legal acts. Specific research projects promoted by this resolution include glacial mass balance predictions under climate change, and hydrological forecasting to ensure the suitability of river systems for hydropower installation.

Document Title: Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
Family Title: Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy
Family Summary: The Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy aims to guide national development in the long term, with a wide range of priority directions and quantified aims across sectors. It aims to reduce the carbon intensity of the economy (emissions per unit GDP) by 30% compared to 2010, increase renewables to 40% of generation, enhance energy efficiency, adapt public transport to green fuels, and establish an MRV system covering all greenhouse gases to support emissions trading. On the environment the strategy commits to the creation of 600,000 ha of green space, the reclamation of over 6000 ha of degraded mining land, and achieve essentially total spatial coverage of early warning systems for weather and flooding. It promotes research into climate-resilient high yielding crop varieties, and improved water management systems to adapt to increasing water scarcity.

Document Title: On Measures to Implement a National System of Transparency in the Transition to a Green Economy in the Republic of Uzbekistan PP-213
Family Title: On Measures to Implement a National System of Transparency in the Transition to a Green Economy in the Republic of Uzbekistan PP-213
Family Summary: The resolution aims to enhance Uzbekistan's response to global climate issues by beginning the creation of a national system for monitoring, recording and verification (MRV) of emissions reductions, alongside a national emissions inventory. This includes compiling comprehensive emissions data for the 1990-2023 period.

Document Title: Law on Limiting Greenhouse Gas Emissions ZRU-1073
Family Title: Law on Limiting Greenhouse Gas Emissions ZRU-1073
Family Summary: The Law on Limiting Greenhouse Gas Emissions ZRU-1073 sets a legal framework around emissions reduction. Document Title: Draft Environmental Code of the Republic of Tajikistan
Family Title: Draft Environmental Code of the Republic of Tajikistan
Family Summary:
The Environmental Code of the Republic of Tajikistan provides a legislative framework and overarching direction for environmental protection, establishing essential duties and responsibilities of the state and other actors.It compiles and builds on existing environmental legislation. The code names climate change mitigation and adaptation as key elements of the protection of the environment, over which the state has legal responsibility, and notes climate change as a key environmental research area. It acknowledges the threat of climate change more broadly across the economy, emphasising the need for action across sectors.

Government statements from September and December 2025 confirm and schedule that the code, subject to possible minor revisions, will be formally approved in early 2026.

Document Title: Law amending the law of 29 April 1999 on the organization of the electricity market
Family Title: Act on Organization of the Electricity Market, amended by law of 12-may-19
Family Summary: The Act regulates organisation of the electricity market and contributes to meeting international commitments related to climate change. This is to be done in particular through promotion of renewable electricity generation, among others by providing federal feed-in tariffs, and organising a federal green certificate scheme. It defines the extensive competences of CREG (the Commission for Regulation of Electricity and Gas) in fixing transport and distribution tariffs, as well as regulating the prices of energy to prevent adverse price increases. The Act further guarantees connection of renewable electricity sources to the grid. It also supports the promotion of renewable energies in planning for electricity sources choice, lays down provisions for feed-in tariffs for renewable electricity production not addressed by specific regional regulation, mandates the federal Minister for Energy to stimulate tenders for renewable electricity generation installations and especially wind power, provides for adoption of specific regulation organizing the green certification scheme. The federal green certificate scheme is further detailed in the Royal order on the creation of a mechanism to support electricity production from renewable energy sources of 2012 (modifying previous regulation from 2002). The Order requires electricity transmission system operators to purchase green or CHP energy certificates at a guaranteed minimum price. Renewable energy facilities (offshore wind farms, PV facilities commissioned before 01/08/2012, hydro or tidal energy facilities and geothermal energy generation facilities) are entitled to receive this support for 10 years after the facility is commissioned. The Act was amended in 2019 by the law on the organisation of the electricity market with a view to introducing a competitive tendering procedure for the construction and operation of production facilities in the marine areas under the jurisdiction of Belgium and ratifying the Royal Decree of 11 February 2019, amending the Royal Decree of 16 July 2002 on the establishment of mechanisms to promote electricity produced from renewable energy sources.

Document Title: Sri Lanka's Coastal Zone and Coastal Resource Management Plan (CZ&CRMP) for 2024- 2029
Family Title: Sri Lanka's Coastal Zone and Coastal Resource Management Plan (CZ&CRMP) for 2024- 2029
Family Summary:
This plan plans to build on post-conflict opportunities to boost the wellbeing of coastal communities. It focuses on shoreline management, conserving coastal habitats, control coastal water pollution, deal with special management areas, and improve regulatory mechanisms. It notably devise strategic schemes to combat floods, sea-level rise and storms. It mandates the country to combat erosion notably by adopting climate compatible technologies and designs for fisheries, tourism and other economic activities located in coastal zones. It also calls for protecting mangroves in order to protect the coast from erosion and ensure carbon storing capabilities. The plan was updated for the 2024-2029 period, in broad alignment. The plan also aims to ensure the availability of contingency measures to mitigate impacts of climate change on coastal features, infrastructure and coastal communities and that systems for timely implementation of such contingency measures and plans are developed. It lists the following proposed actions:

  1. Collate data from all relevant authorities on climate change parameters such as wind patterns, rainfall, temperature, sea level rise, etc. to predict coastal impacts of sea level rise.
  2. establish a database on climate change features relevant to coastal zone management in collaboration with relevant state organisations.
  3. establish links with international agencies/global programmes to obtain data and information on climate change, related features and mitigatory actions.
  4. analyse impacts of climate change and establish systems for timely adaptive and mitigatory action.
  5. Develop an effective mechanism to collaborate with institutions dealing with the scientific and social aspects of natural hazards to minimise impacts and for efficient remedial action.
  6. Coordinate inter-agency action required to mitigate impacts of natural hazards in the Coastal Zone and for remedial measures.
  7. establish a mechanism through which realistic estimates of sea level rise and other climate change impacts are taken into account routinely in erosion management and development in the Coastal Zone.

Document Title: Carbon Net Zero 2050 Roadmap and Strategic Plan
Family Title: Carbon Net Zero 2050 Roadmap and Strategic Plan
Family Summary:
The Roadmap and Strategic Plan provide a broad and detailed guiding framework for the achievement of net-zero emissions in Sri Lanka by 2050, to be achieved by emissions reductions and expanding forest-based sequestration.

As immediate specific government priorities it promotes: review and update of nuclear energy regulation to facilitate projects; finalising the national transport policy; sustainability guidelines mainstreamed into industrial park development; developing policies for district heating and co-generation; introducing landfill gas recovery to the national waste management policy; introduction of waste-to-energy facilities; enhance legislation and enforcement around general NDC implementations; introduce mandatory household waste segregation; policy emphasis on agricultural renewable energy and fertiliser/water use in the coconut industry.

On the sequestration end, the plan promotes an afforestation/restoration/reforestation rate of 25,000 ha per year up to 2030, also halting any losses to urban tree cover. These figures include plantation trees.

Document Title: National Policy on forests
Family Title: National Policy on Forests
Family Summary:
The National Policy on Forests (1997) sets Poland’s long-term framework for sustainable forest management, balancing timber production with biodiversity, ecological protection, and social uses. It promotes increasing forest cover and forest resilience while integrating ecological, economic, and social objectives. In the LULUCF sector, forests contribute to carbon sequestration, with short-term increases projected, though long-term accumulation may decline due to aging stands, slower growth, and climate-related stress.

By combining sustainable management, biodiversity protection, and climate-related considerations, the National Policy on Forests contributes to short-term carbon mitigation and lays the groundwork for resilient, multifunctional forest ecosystems in the face of climate change and environmental pressures

Document Title: Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (2021–2027)
Family Title: Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (2021–2027)
Family Summary:
The Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (Plan przeciwdziałania skutkom suszy (PPSS)) is the first national planning document addressing the issue of minimizing the effects of drought. Its development stemmed from the provisions of EU directives and guidelines (the Water Framework Directive) as well as national law (Article 184 of the Water Law Act). It was adopted by the Regulation of the Minister of Infrastructure on 15 July 2021 (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1615).

It provides a comprehensive analysis of drought risk, outlines proposals to increase available water resources, enhance natural and artificial retention, and sets out a detailed catalogue of measures to reduce the impacts of drought on society, the economy and the environment. The plan is structured around four specific goals: effective water resource management, increasing water retention, education and coordination on drought issues, and mechanisms for implementation and financing. While not an investment plan itself, PPSS includes proposals for water infrastructure projects and retention solutions and complements other national water-management planning instruments, helping improve resilience to drought and secure water availability.

Document Title: Amendment Act of 27 November 2024
Family Title: Act of 20 February 2015 on renewable energy sources, last amended by Act of 9 October 2025 (RES Act)
Family Summary:
This Act defines the new regime for support to renewable energy sources (including wind energy, energy radiation of the sun, solar, aerothermal, geothermal, hydrothermal energy, hydropower, waves, currents error and tidal energy obtained from biomass, biogas, agricultural biogas and bioliquid - art. 2.22), aiming to stabilise the long-term support system, with the goal to prevent electricity prices form increasing in an uncontrolled manner. The Act also transposes the Directive 2009/28/EC on renewable energy into Polish legislation and aims to contribute to Poland's target of reaching 15% share of renewable energy production by 2020. The Act will provide continuing support to most existing installations (in operation by or before 31 December 2015) through certificates of origin, while future investments will compete for support through an auction system organised by the President of the Energy Regulatory Office (ERO). The auctions, applying to new installations over 10 kW of installed capacity, will be based on a type of contract-for-difference (CfD) granted, with separate auctions for old and new plants and for plants of 1 MW or less, as well as varied reference prices for the eighteen renewable sources reference groups. The chosen renewable plants will have to start generation within 24 months (solar plants), 72 months (wind plants) or 48 months (others), and they will be required to deliver at least 85% of the volume offered in the bid, under threat of penalty. The energy auctioned will be bought by the newly formed state-owned entity Operator Rozlicze? Energii Odnawialnej (for energy produced in installations above 500kW) or by electricity distribution companies (for energy produced in installations up to 500kW). Most existing installations will also be eligible to change to the auction support instrument from the current certificates of origin, except for hydropower plants over 5 MW, non-qualified biomass co-firing installations (art. 44) and biomass installations exceeding 50 MW of electrical power (or 150 MW of CHP power). The existing installations will continue to be eligible for the existing system of support through certificates of origin (introduced through the 1997 Energy Law), but a number of limits will apply:

  • support for max 15 years from the start of renewable energy production in the given installation;
  • support for hydropower of max 5 MW of capacity;
  • support for biomass co-firing installations of less than 150 MW capacity capped to equivalent of the average generation over 2011-2013;
  • large consumers (over 100 GWh of electricity consumed annually) and commodity brokerage houses are required to obtain certificates of origin for 14% and 15% of their annual electricity consumption for 2015 and 2016 respectively or pay the substitution fee. From 2017 the share is min 20%, but can be reduced by the Minister of Economy, if necessary due to specific market conditions. A unit substitution fee is set to a constant 300.03 PLN/MWh (2014 level, approx. 72 €/MWh), which should stabilise the price of certificates, as purchasing and redeeming of certificates of origin will only be allowed if the average market price of certificates remains below 75% of the substitution fee.

The Act also introduces a feed-in tariff system for micro installations of up to 10 kW (max 40 kW under special conditions - art. 41.7), while guaranteeing purchase by electricity distribution companies at 100% of market price for the next 15 years, until no later than December 31, 2035 (art. 41.5). The support also covers the so-called ‘prosumers,' who both produce and consume their own electricity. The subsidies amount to PLN 0.75 (EUR 0.18) per kWh to prosumers with a capacity of up to 3 kW (hydropower, wind, solar), and PLN 0.40-0.70 (EUR 0.10-0.17) for those with a capacity between 3 and 10 kW (biogas, hydropower, wind, solar). Moreover, there are no licensing/concession requirements for those micro generators that do not have active business. The Act was amended in June 2018, alongside the 2016 Act on investments in wind power and the 1994 Construction Act, in order to boost offshore wind investment. It was further amended in August 2019 to extend the agreements on grid connection and updates the auction mechanism.The Act was notably amended by bill 1129/2021 to extend the period for auctions of energy sales, set auction volumes, and remove obligations for small producers of renewable energy. The Amendments from November 2024 and October 2025 to the Renewable Energy Sources Act represent a strategic pivot toward "energy democratization," fundamentally increasing the profitability and accessibility of green energy. The November 2024 Act introduced a more favorable "net-billing" calculation and cut administrative wait times for solar building permits and grid connections from months to just 30 to 45 days. The October 2025 Act expanded these rights to urban dwellers by allowing energy cooperatives to operate in cities and granting "tenant prosumers" the flexibility to install solar panels on carports and garages rather than just roofs. Together, these laws establish renewable energy as an "overriding public interest".

Document Title: Resolution No. 149 on the National Policy Framework for the Development of the Market for Alternative Fuels in the Transport Sector and the Development of the Relevant Infrastructure
Family Title: Resolution No. 149/2025 on the National Policy Framework for the Development of the Market for Alternative Fuels in the Transport Sector and the Development of the Relevant Infrastructure
Family Summary:
The National Policy Framework for the Development of the Alternative Fuels Market, adopted via Resolution No. 149, serves as Poland's strategic roadmap to decarbonize the transport sector and align with the European Union’s AFIR requirements. Its primary objective is the massive expansion of charging and refueling infrastructure, aiming for approximately 87,000 public electric vehicle charging points by 2030, with a specific focus on installing high-power stations every 60 km along major TEN-T highway corridors. Beyond electrification, the framework prioritizes the development of a hydrogen refueling network for heavy-duty transport, the implementation of shore-side electricity for ships at major maritime ports, and the integration of sustainable fuels in aviation. Ultimately, the policy seeks to eliminate technical barriers, while providing the financial subsidies and regulatory stability necessary to transition Poland's logistics and transit industries toward a zero-emission future.

It also aims to establish a network of 37 hydrogen refueling stations by 2030 to support a projected fleet of over 1,000 hydrogen-powered buses and heavy trucks, while simultaneously promoting biomethane as a renewable drop-in replacement for natural gas to decarbonize existing CNG and LNG infrastructure.

Document Title: Flood Risk Management Plan (PZRP): River basin: Danube
Family Title: Flood Risk Management Plan (PZRP): River basin: Danube
Family Summary:
Directive 2007/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2007 on the assessment and management of flood risks (Floods Directive) requires, among other things, the preparation of flood risk management plans. The President of the National Water Management Authority is responsible for developing flood risk management plans in accordance with the Water Law Act.

The Flood Risk Management Plan (PZRP) encompasses all elements of flood risk management, with particular emphasis on flood prevention and protection measures, as well as information on the state of preparedness in the event of a flood. Pursuant to the Water Law Act, flood protection is implemented in a manner that ensures coordination with activities aimed at achieving environmental and water protection objectives. Flood Risk Management Plans (PZRP) were developed for 6 river basins.

The Regulation of the Council of Ministers of 18 October 2022 adopted the Flood Risk Management Plan for the Danube river basin, which entered into force on 23.12.2022.

Document Title: Act 3 of October 2008 (EIA Act) - Initial text

Family Summary: The EIA Act establishes Poland’s legal framework for access to environmental information, public participation in environmental protection and environmental impact assessment (EIA) procedures. It guarantees that environmental information (e.g., data on pollution, plans and decisions) is made available to the public and sets out how citizens and organisations can participate in environmental decision‑making. It also implements EU and international law on environmental impact assessments by defining the scope and procedures for assessing the likely environmental effects of proposed projects and plansLastly, the act states that the EIA report shall include a description of the likely significant effects of the project on the air, water, soil, climate, fauna, flora, landscape and cultural heritage, including transboundary effects and estimate of emissions, including greenhouse gases, and a description of the measures planned to prevent, reduce or offset adverse environmental impacts.

Family Summary:

The excise tax exemption applies to electric, hydrogen (indefinite) and plug-in hybrid vehicles with an internal combustion engine capacity not exceeding 2000 cm³ (timely exemption).

Currently, pursuant to the Act of 1 December 2022 amending the Act of 06 December 2008 on Excise Duty and certain other acts (Journal of Laws item 2707), the excise duty exemption previously in force until 31 December 2022 for passenger cars that are plug-in hybrid vehicles with an internal combustion engine capacity not exceeding 2000 cm³ has been extended until 31 December 2029. Document Title: Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy
Family Title: Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy
Family Summary:
The UK's goal for domestic maritime is to aim for zero fuel lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050, with at least a 30% reduction by 2030 and an 80% reduction by 2040, relative to 2008 levels. This Strategy, aligned with the International Maritime Organisation's GHG Strategy, sets out the pathway to meet the goals, providing certainty and clarity for the maritime sector. This Strategy is accompanied by an Analytical Index which sets out the usefulness of policy interventions against modelling scenarios.

The five key policies are: introduce new regulation to increase the use of clean maritime fuels, place a price on GHG emissions, consider how best to reduce GHG emissions from vessels at berth, set out how the UK will support all vessels, regardless of size, to decarbonise, and improve the energy efficiency of vessels.

The UK expects to publish a refresh of this Strategy within five years, updating its goals and policy interventions as their evidence base increases in size and robustness.

Document Title: Amending Act of 9 October 2025

Family Summary: The Polish Water Law establishes an integrated framework for managing water resources with strong relevance for climate adaptation, energy security, and disaster risk management. It explicitly addresses climate-related pressures by prioritising protection against floods and droughts, introducing risk-based planning, flood hazard and risk mapping, and the use of retention, polders, and coastal protection infrastructure to reduce climate-driven extremes. Document Title: Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (2021–2027) - Non Specialist version
Family Title: Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (2021–2027)
Family Summary:
The Polish National Plan for Counteracting the Effects of Drought (Plan przeciwdziałania skutkom suszy (PPSS)) is the first national planning document addressing the issue of minimizing the effects of drought. Its development stemmed from the provisions of EU directives and guidelines (the Water Framework Directive) as well as national law (Article 184 of the Water Law Act). It was adopted by the Regulation of the Minister of Infrastructure on 15 July 2021 (Dz.U. 2021 poz. 1615).

It provides a comprehensive analysis of drought risk, outlines proposals to increase available water resources, enhance natural and artificial retention, and sets out a detailed catalogue of measures to reduce the impacts of drought on society, the economy and the environment. The plan is structured around four specific goals: effective water resource management, increasing water retention, education and coordination on drought issues, and mechanisms for implementation and financing. While not an investment plan itself, PPSS includes proposals for water infrastructure projects and retention solutions and complements other national water-management planning instruments, helping improve resilience to drought and secure water availability.

Document Title: Coastal Zone and Coastal Resource Management Plan 2018
Family Title: Sri Lanka's Coastal Zone and Coastal Resource Management Plan (CZ&CRMP) for 2024- 2029
Family Summary:
This plan plans to build on post-conflict opportunities to boost the wellbeing of coastal communities. It focuses on shoreline management, conserving coastal habitats, control coastal water pollution, deal with special management areas, and improve regulatory mechanisms. It notably devise strategic schemes to combat floods, sea-level rise and storms. It mandates the country to combat erosion notably by adopting climate compatible technologies and designs for fisheries, tourism and other economic activities located in coastal zones. It also calls for protecting mangroves in order to protect the coast from erosion and ensure carbon storing capabilities. The plan was updated for the 2024-2029 period, in broad alignment. The plan also aims to ensure the availability of contingency measures to mitigate impacts of climate change on coastal features, infrastructure and coastal communities and that systems for timely implementation of such contingency measures and plans are developed. It lists the following proposed actions:

  1. Collate data from all relevant authorities on climate change parameters such as wind patterns, rainfall, temperature, sea level rise, etc. to predict coastal impacts of sea level rise.
  2. establish a database on climate change features relevant to coastal zone management in collaboration with relevant state organisations.
  3. establish links with international agencies/global programmes to obtain data and information on climate change, related features and mitigatory actions.
  4. analyse impacts of climate change and establish systems for timely adaptive and mitigatory action.
  5. Develop an effective mechanism to collaborate with institutions dealing with the scientific and social aspects of natural hazards to minimise impacts and for efficient remedial action.
  6. Coordinate inter-agency action required to mitigate impacts of natural hazards in the Coastal Zone and for remedial measures.
  7. establish a mechanism through which realistic estimates of sea level rise and other climate change impacts are taken into account routinely in erosion management and development in the Coastal Zone.

Family Title: Act of 25 August 2006 on biocomponents and liquid biofuels, last amended by Act of 21 February 2025
Family Summary: This Act (last amended in January 2015) establishes that the producers, importers and suppliers of fuels are obliged to meet an annual quota of biofuels in the total amount of liquid fuels produced, supplied and imported. Document Title: Amending Act of 21 November 2025
Family Title: Act of 17 July 2009 on the system for managing emissions of greenhouse gases and other substances,  last amended by Act of 21 November 2025
Family Summary:
This Act introduces the legal basis for the management of national GHG emissions and other substances in order to fulfill Poland's obligations towards the EU and the UNFCCC. It allows pollution to be cut in the cheapest possible way and it introduces into Polish law the three mechanisms under the Kyoto Protocol: Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation This Act sets forth the following: - Responsibilities of the National Centre for Emission Balancing and Management; - The principles of the operation of the National System for Emission Balancing and Forecasting; - The principles of the management of emissions of GHGs and other substances; - The principles of the operation of the National Registry of the Kyoto Units and emission allowance; - The principles of trading in and managing the Kyoto units; - The principles of the operation of the National Green Investment Scheme and the Climate Account; - The terms and conditions of the management of the Joint Implementation projects in the territory of the Republic of Poland; and - The terms and conditions of the management outside the territory of the Republic of Poland for the Joint Implementation projects, and the Clean Development Mechanism projects. Projects implemented in following areas can be considered for implementation under the GIS Act: (i) energy efficiency; (ii) clean coal technologies; (iii) replacement of high-emission by low-emission fuel; (iv) avoidance or reduction of GHG emissions from the transport sector; (v) use of renewable energy sources; (vi) avoidance or reduction of methane emissions through recycling and use in power generation; (vii) GHG sequestration; (viii) actions to reduce or avoid GHG emissions, to absorb CO2 and adapt to climate change; (ix) research and development of renewable energy sources and advanced and innovative environmentally-friendly technologies; (x) educational activities.

The 2025 amendment (Dz.U. 2025 poz. 1863) to the Act of 17 July 2009 on the System to Manage the Emissions of Greenhouse Gases and Other Substances introduces several updates mainly to align Polish law with EU carbon-border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) and related EU requirements, and to strengthen administrative cooperation and enforcement: the amendment adds new EU legal references (including an EU Commission implementing decision) in the Act’s reference section and updates the scope of tasks of environmental and customs authorities so that they support implementation of CBAM reporting.

Document Title: Act of 20 February 2015 on renewable energy sources, last amended by Act of 9 October 2025 (Consolidated text)
Family Title: Act of 20 February 2015 on renewable energy sources, last amended by Act of 9 October 2025 (RES Act)
Family Summary:
This Act defines the new regime for support to renewable energy sources (including wind energy, energy radiation of the sun, solar, aerothermal, geothermal, hydrothermal energy, hydropower, waves, currents error and tidal energy obtained from biomass, biogas, agricultural biogas and bioliquid - art. 2.22), aiming to stabilise the long-term support system, with the goal to prevent electricity prices form increasing in an uncontrolled manner. The Act also transposes the Directive 2009/28/EC on renewable energy into Polish legislation and aims to contribute to Poland's target of reaching 15% share of renewable energy production by 2020. The Act will provide continuing support to most existing installations (in operation by or before 31 December 2015) through certificates of origin, while future investments will compete for support through an auction system organised by the President of the Energy Regulatory Office (ERO). The auctions, applying to new installations over 10 kW of installed capacity, will be based on a type of contract-for-difference (CfD) granted, with separate auctions for old and new plants and for plants of 1 MW or less, as well as varied reference prices for the eighteen renewable sources reference groups. The chosen renewable plants will have to start generation within 24 months (solar plants), 72 months (wind plants) or 48 months (others), and they will be required to deliver at least 85% of the volume offered in the bid, under threat of penalty. The energy auctioned will be bought by the newly formed state-owned entity Operator Rozlicze? Energii Odnawialnej (for energy produced in installations above 500kW) or by electricity distribution companies (for energy produced in installations up to 500kW). Most existing installations will also be eligible to change to the auction support instrument from the current certificates of origin, except for hydropower plants over 5 MW, non-qualified biomass co-firing installations (art. 44) and biomass installations exceeding 50 MW of electrical power (or 150 MW of CHP power). The existing installations will continue to be eligible for the existing system of support through certificates of origin (introduced through the 1997 Energy Law), but a number of limits will apply:

  • support for max 15 years from the start of renewable energy production in the given installation;
  • support for hydropower of max 5 MW of capacity;
  • support for biomass co-firing installations of less than 150 MW capacity capped to equivalent of the average generation over 2011-2013;
  • large consumers (over 100 GWh of electricity consumed annually) and commodity brokerage houses are required to obtain certificates of origin for 14% and 15% of their annual electricity consumption for 2015 and 2016 respectively or pay the substitution fee. From 2017 the share is min 20%, but can be reduced by the Minister of Economy, if necessary due to specific market conditions. A unit substitution fee is set to a constant 300.03 PLN/MWh (2014 level, approx. 72 €/MWh), which should stabilise the price of certificates, as purchasing and redeeming of certificates of origin will only be allowed if the average market price of certificates remains below 75% of the substitution fee.

The Act also introduces a feed-in tariff system for micro installations of up to 10 kW (max 40 kW under special conditions - art. 41.7), while guaranteeing purchase by electricity distribution companies at 100% of market price for the next 15 years, until no later than December 31, 2035 (art. 41.5). The support also covers the so-called ‘prosumers,' who both produce and consume their own electricity. The subsidies amount to PLN 0.75 (EUR 0.18) per kWh to prosumers with a capacity of up to 3 kW (hydropower, wind, solar), and PLN 0.40-0.70 (EUR 0.10-0.17) for those with a capacity between 3 and 10 kW (biogas, hydropower, wind, solar). Moreover, there are no licensing/concession requirements for those micro generators that do not have active business. The Act was amended in June 2018, alongside the 2016 Act on investments in wind power and the 1994 Construction Act, in order to boost offshore wind investment. It was further amended in August 2019 to extend the agreements on grid connection and updates the auction mechanism.The Act was notably amended by bill 1129/2021 to extend the period for auctions of energy sales, set auction volumes, and remove obligations for small producers of renewable energy. The Amendments from November 2024 and October 2025 to the Renewable Energy Sources Act represent a strategic pivot toward "energy democratization," fundamentally increasing the profitability and accessibility of green energy. The November 2024 Act introduced a more favorable "net-billing" calculation and cut administrative wait times for solar building permits and grid connections from months to just 30 to 45 days. The October 2025 Act expanded these rights to urban dwellers by allowing energy cooperatives to operate in cities and granting "tenant prosumers" the flexibility to install solar panels on carports and garages rather than just roofs. Together, these laws establish renewable energy as an "overriding public interest".

Document Title: Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy - Analytical Annex
Family Title: Maritime Decarbonisation Strategy
Family Summary:
The UK's goal for domestic maritime is to aim for zero fuel lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050, with at least a 30% reduction by 2030 and an 80% reduction by 2040, relative to 2008 levels. This Strategy, aligned with the International Maritime Organisation's GHG Strategy, sets out the pathway to meet the goals, providing certainty and clarity for the maritime sector. This Strategy is accompanied by an Analytical Index which sets out the usefulness of policy interventions against modelling scenarios.

The five key policies are: introduce new regulation to increase the use of clean maritime fuels, place a price on GHG emissions, consider how best to reduce GHG emissions from vessels at berth, set out how the UK will support all vessels, regardless of size, to decarbonise, and improve the energy efficiency of vessels.

The UK expects to publish a refresh of this Strategy within five years, updating its goals and policy interventions as their evidence base increases in size and robustness.

Document Title: Amending Act of 9 October 2025
Family Title: Act of 10 April 1997- Energy Law
Family Summary: This law (with later amendments, lastly in September 2015) defines the principles of state energy policy, conditions for the supply and use of fuels and energy, and the framework for activities of energy companies. It also specifies the authorities responsible for the management of fuels and energy. Among others, it established the basis for independent electricity and gas production and access of independent power producers to the grid, principles for least cost and integrated resource planning, support to high efficiency heat and power production, demand side management and energy efficiency labels. It facilities the production of electricity from renewable energy sources (up to 5MW), making them eligible to benefit from a reduced grid connection fee and exempt from paying annual licence fees. Energy providers are allowed to incorporate costs of developing renewable energy into their tariff regimes. Since 1 October 2005, energy enterprises that generate, trade or purchase electricity are obliged to purchase or generate a certain amount of electricity from renewable sources of energy. The obligation will be met through the acquisition and redemption of certificates of origin that certify electricity produced from renewable sources. Transmissions and distribution operators are obliged to accept renewable sources of energy. Similar scheme for heat produced from renewable energy sources entered into force on 1 January 2007. The amendment of 26 July of 2013 simplified the setting up a micro-installation (renewable energy sources with no more than 40kW of total installed electrical capacity, connected to electrical grid of a voltage lower than 110kV or no more than 120 kW of total installed heat capacity). Applications to connect a micro-installation to the grid will no longer be subject to a connection fee nor required to attach documents confirming the admissibility of locating the installation in the investment area. In some cases, there will be no need for an interconnection agreement. It also expands the definition of renewable energy sources to aerothermal and hydrothermal, it provides the protection of vulnerable consumers, as well as support for energy-intensive industries. In order to make the gas market more transparent and competitive, the Small Tri-Pack imposes the obligation to sell at least 30% (40% since 2014 and 55% since 2015) of the gas at the exchange markets. The Act also exempts people producing energy from renewable resources for their own purposes from the obligation to obtain the license for the power supply. The amendment to the Energy Law from 26 September 2015 introduces measures necessary for the application of the 'REMIT Regulation' of the European Parliament and the Council Regulation no. 1227/2011 (25 October 2011) on the wholesale energy market integrity and transparency. It establishes a legal framework necessary for monitoring the practices of wholesale energy market participants, as well as detecting and deterring fraudulent practices in this sector.The "meter Act" of June 2021 amends this document and others to boost the deployment of smart meters in the country.In 2025, the Polish Energy Law was modified by multiple amendments to strengthen legal clarity, market functioning and support for the energy transition: the Act of 5 August 2025 updated the Energy Law itself and related statutes to address structural issues arising from corporate reorganisations (ensuring that obligations of reserve sellers and default sellers automatically transfer to successor companies after a corporate division), clarified how supplier duties carry over after such a division, and aligned transitional rules for obligated sellers in electricity and gas markets with ongoing company changes; this reform aimed to close legal gaps around entity succession and ensure continuity of supply and regulatory obligations following company splits. At the same time, the October amendment to the Offshore Wind Promotion Act also amended the Energy Law (among other statutes) to incorporate provisions facilitating renewable energy development, such as improving the grid connection regime for offshore wind farms, allowing shared use of offshore electrical infrastructure. These amendments both tighten control over conventional energy markets and simultaneously create a more enabling legal framework for renewable energy development, supporting Poland’s energy security and decarbonisation goals.

Family Title: Act of 17 July 2009 on the system for managing emissions of greenhouse gases and other substances,  last amended by Act of 21 November 2025
Family Summary:
This Act introduces the legal basis for the management of national GHG emissions and other substances in order to fulfill Poland's obligations towards the EU and the UNFCCC. It allows pollution to be cut in the cheapest possible way and it introduces into Polish law the three mechanisms under the Kyoto Protocol: Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation This Act sets forth the following: - Responsibilities of the National Centre for Emission Balancing and Management; - The principles of the operation of the National System for Emission Balancing and Forecasting; - The principles of the management of emissions of GHGs and other substances; - The principles of the operation of the National Registry of the Kyoto Units and emission allowance; - The principles of trading in and managing the Kyoto units; - The principles of the operation of the National Green Investment Scheme and the Climate Account; - The terms and conditions of the management of the Joint Implementation projects in the territory of the Republic of Poland; and - The terms and conditions of the management outside the territory of the Republic of Poland for the Joint Implementation projects, and the Clean Development Mechanism projects. Projects implemented in following areas can be considered for implementation under the GIS Act: (i) energy efficiency; (ii) clean coal technologies; (iii) replacement of high-emission by low-emission fuel; (iv) avoidance or reduction of GHG emissions from the transport sector; (v) use of renewable energy sources; (vi) avoidance or reduction of methane emissions through recycling and use in power generation; (vii) GHG sequestration; (viii) actions to reduce or avoid GHG emissions, to absorb CO2 and adapt to climate change; (ix) research and development of renewable energy sources and advanced and innovative environmentally-friendly technologies; (x) educational activities.

The 2025 amendment (Dz.U. 2025 poz. 1863) to the Act of 17 July 2009 on the System to Manage the Emissions of Greenhouse Gases and Other Substances introduces several updates mainly to align Polish law with EU carbon-border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) and related EU requirements, and to strengthen administrative cooperation and enforcement: the amendment adds new EU legal references (including an EU Commission implementing decision) in the Act’s reference section and updates the scope of tasks of environmental and customs authorities so that they support implementation of CBAM reporting.

Document Title: Act of 20 February 2015 on renewable energy sources (Initial text)
Family Title: Act of 20 February 2015 on renewable energy sources, last amended by Act of 9 October 2025 (RES Act)
Family Summary:
This Act defines the new regime for support to renewable energy sources (including wind energy, energy radiation of the sun, solar, aerothermal, geothermal, hydrothermal energy, hydropower, waves, currents error and tidal energy obtained from biomass, biogas, agricultural biogas and bioliquid - art. 2.22), aiming to stabilise the long-term support system, with the goal to prevent electricity prices form increasing in an uncontrolled manner. The Act also transposes the Directive 2009/28/EC on renewable energy into Polish legislation and aims to contribute to Poland's target of reaching 15% share of renewable energy production by 2020. The Act will provide continuing support to most existing installations (in operation by or before 31 December 2015) through certificates of origin, while future investments will compete for support through an auction system organised by the President of the Energy Regulatory Office (ERO). The auctions, applying to new installations over 10 kW of installed capacity, will be based on a type of contract-for-difference (CfD) granted, with separate auctions for old and new plants and for plants of 1 MW or less, as well as varied reference prices for the eighteen renewable sources reference groups. The chosen renewable plants will have to start generation within 24 months (solar plants), 72 months (wind plants) or 48 months (others), and they will be required to deliver at least 85% of the volume offered in the bid, under threat of penalty. The energy auctioned will be bought by the newly formed state-owned entity Operator Rozlicze? Energii Odnawialnej (for energy produced in installations above 500kW) or by electricity distribution companies (for energy produced in installations up to 500kW). Most existing installations will also be eligible to change to the auction support instrument from the current certificates of origin, except for hydropower plants over 5 MW, non-qualified biomass co-firing installations (art. 44) and biomass installations exceeding 50 MW of electrical power (or 150 MW of CHP power). The existing installations will continue to be eligible for the existing system of support through certificates of origin (introduced through the 1997 Energy Law), but a number of limits will apply:

  • support for max 15 years from the start of renewable energy production in the given installation;
  • support for hydropower of max 5 MW of capacity;
  • support for biomass co-firing installations of less than 150 MW capacity capped to equivalent of the average generation over 2011-2013;
  • large consumers (over 100 GWh of electricity consumed annually) and commodity brokerage houses are required to obtain certificates of origin for 14% and 15% of their annual electricity consumption for 2015 and 2016 respectively or pay the substitution fee. From 2017 the share is min 20%, but can be reduced by the Minister of Economy, if necessary due to specific market conditions. A unit substitution fee is set to a constant 300.03 PLN/MWh (2014 level, approx. 72 €/MWh), which should stabilise the price of certificates, as purchasing and redeeming of certificates of origin will only be allowed if the average market price of certificates remains below 75% of the substitution fee.

The Act also introduces a feed-in tariff system for micro installations of up to 10 kW (max 40 kW under special conditions - art. 41.7), while guaranteeing purchase by electricity distribution companies at 100% of market price for the next 15 years, until no later than December 31, 2035 (art. 41.5). The support also covers the so-called ‘prosumers,' who both produce and consume their own electricity. The subsidies amount to PLN 0.75 (EUR 0.18) per kWh to prosumers with a capacity of up to 3 kW (hydropower, wind, solar), and PLN 0.40-0.70 (EUR 0.10-0.17) for those with a capacity between 3 and 10 kW (biogas, hydropower, wind, solar). Moreover, there are no licensing/concession requirements for those micro generators that do not have active business. The Act was amended in June 2018, alongside the 2016 Act on investments in wind power and the 1994 Construction Act, in order to boost offshore wind investment. It was further amended in August 2019 to extend the agreements on grid connection and updates the auction mechanism.The Act was notably amended by bill 1129/2021 to extend the period for auctions of energy sales, set auction volumes, and remove obligations for small producers of renewable energy. The Amendments from November 2024 and October 2025 to the Renewable Energy Sources Act represent a strategic pivot toward "energy democratization," fundamentally increasing the profitability and accessibility of green energy. The November 2024 Act introduced a more favorable "net-billing" calculation and cut administrative wait times for solar building permits and grid connections from months to just 30 to 45 days. The October 2025 Act expanded these rights to urban dwellers by allowing energy cooperatives to operate in cities and granting "tenant prosumers" the flexibility to install solar panels on carports and garages rather than just roofs. Together, these laws establish renewable energy as an "overriding public interest".

Document Title: Act of 14 December 2018 on the promotion of electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration (the CHP Act)  - Initial text
Family Title: Act of 14 December 2018 on the promotion of electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration, last amended by Act of 27 November 2024 (CHP Act)
Family Summary:
This act is centred around the promotion of electricity from high-efficiency cogeneration through a support scheme in the form of cogeneration bonus (CHP auction) for electricity generators from high-efficiency cogeneration.

This subsidy scheme is approved by the Polish Ministry of Climate and Environment, the Consultative Council of the Modernization Fund and the European Investment Bank. It totals an allocation of PLN 1.5 Billion aimed at co/financing the development of cogeneration with municipal biogas in the form of grant or loans covering 50% or 100% of eligible costs respectively. It supports the construction of new installations, or the extension or modernization of existing installations, for the fermentation of municipal organic waste and the use of the obtained biogas to generate energy through high-efficiency cogeneration.

Applications from companies are open from February to June in 2024, and are covering costs from September 2022 up to December 2030.The Act of 27 November 2024 updated provisions relevant to cogeneration in the context of industrial customer eligibility for renewables‑related entitlements and compliance obligations — notably by aligning the conditions for industrial consumers to benefit from exemptions or support under the cogeneration law with new renewable energy criteria, such as demonstrating reductions in greenhouse gas emissions or improvements in energy efficiency, and requiring updated attestations and documentation for eligibility in 2025. These changes reflect the integration of high‑efficiency cogeneration support with broader renewable energy and energy‑intensive consumer rules established in the amended Renewable Energy Sources Act.

Document Title: Law No. 2025-528 of 25 June 2025 on combating climate change
Family Title: Law No. 2025-528 of 25 June 2025 on combating climate change
Family Summary:
This Law seeks to improve climate governance, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, mobilise financing, increase resilience, and integrate vulnerable populations into climate strategies. It lists the obligations of the State, the local authorities, the private sector, civil society and individuals in respect of combating climate change. The government is to formulate the national policies, strategies and plans on mitigation and adaptation.

This Law lists mitigation measures in various sectors, including agriculture, forestry and land use, energy, transport, buildings, waste and industry, and adaptation measures in relation to agriculture, forestry and land use, water, coastal erosion, and disaster risk management, health, the urban environment, and tourism.

The Law provides for the establishment of a government organisation to combat climate change, with the details to be determined by ministerial decree.

There are also provisions on capacity-building and education, research and development, and participation in carbon markets.

Family Title: Sectoral Adaptation Programme (SAP) on Agriculture 2025-2030
Family Summary: The Sectoral Adaptation Programme (SAP) on Agriculture for 2025-2030 provides a climate vulnerability analysis and recommended actions to ensure effective adaptation to climate change in the agricultural sector. It emphasises issues around water availability and the dependence of the sector on outdated irrigation systems, promoting better surface water collection and storage, covered canals, desalination, crop rotation and the breeding of more stress-tolerant crop varieties. It also promotes broader efforts to build capacity and disseminate information, including integration of agricultural adaptation into education systems and the creation of monitoring systems for soil and air quality. The programme includes an intersection with gender issues, and promotes technical adaptation and better small business infrastructure as tools to mitigate women's heightened vulnerability to climate issues in subsistence farming communities.

Family Summary:
This Strategy identifies climate change as a cross-cutting threat to child well-being. The Action Plan outlines that there is a need for detailed, prioritised assessments and services specific to children in all disaster and crisis situations, including climate change.

Other actions include establishing an international child participation platform on climate change, Zero Waste and efficient use of resources. It is thought that ensuring child participation in the work of public institutions and organisations, and children leading the work in activities related to climate change and sustainability, will contribute to the formation of a generation that builds their own future. Document Title: National Circular Economy Strategy and Action Plan
Family Title: National Circular Economy Strategy and Action Plan
Family Summary: The National Circular Economy Strategy and Action Plan, which contributes towards combating climate change, strengthens the understanding of circular economy in Turkey and to implement environmentally friendly production and consumption models. Circular economy is not only a concept but also our responsibility for the future. With this strategy, Turkey will maximise resource efficiency, ensure the reuse of waste, and create new business and investment opportunities while protecting our environment. The objective is to increase the use of circular materials by minimising waste generation in our production and consumption processes, while achieving the net-zero emissions target by 2053. The action plan will encourage the adoption of environmentally friendly practices at every stage from industrial production to consumption and will instill circular economy awareness in all segments of society. In many sectors, from packaging to textiles, from electronic products to construction, sustainable and environmentally friendly solutions will be developed and these solutions will be integrated into production and consumption processes.

Document Title: Poland’s Recovery and Resilience Plan
Family Title: Poland’s Recovery and Resilience Plan
Family Summary:
To benefit from the support of the Recovery and Resilience Facility set up by the EU in the aftermath of the COVID-19-induced economic crisis, Member States submit their recovery and resilience plans to the European Commission. Each plan sets out the reforms and investments to be implemented by end-2026 and Member States can receive financing up to a previously agreed allocation. Each plan should effectively address challenges identified in the European Semester, particularly the country-specific recommendations of 2019 and 2020 adopted by the Council. It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient.The Total value reaches approx. €59.8 billion, which are divided into (i) €25.3 billion in RRF grants and (ii) €34.5 billion in RRF loans.

Poland’s plan strongly supports climate and environment objectives:

• ≈46.6 % of funding goes to green projects.

• Includes investment in renewable energy (offshore onshore wind), energy-efficient building renovations, green hydrogen, and sustainable transport.

• Regulatory changes to facilitate renewable projects and electricity imports.

The plan was approved by the Council on 17 June 2022.

Document Title: Offshore Wind Roadmap
Family Title: Offshore Wind Roadmap
Family Summary:
This roadmap provides strategic analysis of the offshore wind development potential in Türkiye, considering the opportunities and challenges under different, hypothetical, growth scenarios. It is intended to provide evidence to support the Government of Türkiye in establishing policy, regulations, processes, and infrastructure to enable successful growth of this new industry.

With energy demand expected to continue increasing, Türkiye needs to expand local energy generation to reduce its reliance on imports and the associated foreign exchange burden on its economy. Türkiye has areas with good natural conditions for offshore wind. This offers a new source of domestic renewable energy generation that could contribute to Türkiye’s transition to net-zero carbon by 2053.

The Roadmap recommends 21 actions that mainly focus on actions to be taken in the short term, but some can span over the entire timeframe up to 2050, across the areas of: vision and volume targets; regulatory and policy framework; financial and economic; health and safety; grid and port infrastructure; and supply chain.

Document Title: National Strategy and Action Plan to Combat Desertification (2024-2030)
Family Title: National Strategy and Action Plan to Combat Desertification (2024-2030)
Family Summary:
The National Strategy and Action Plan to Combat Desertification (NSAPCD) outlines Türkiye’s roadmap for combating desertification from 2024 to 2030. Formulated with the active involvement of all relevant stakeholders in desertification mitigation efforts which require an integrated approach, the NSAPCD aligns directly with the Sustainable Development Goal of achieving a “Land Degradation Neutral World.”

The document represents Türkiye’s national implementation of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and it is designed to support the monitoring and reporting of the actions which our country is required to take. Covering national targets up to 2030, the Strategy and Action Plan will make a direct contribution to Türkiye’s overarching goals, including the 2053 net-zero emissions target, particularly through climate change adaptation initiatives. In five dedicated sections, the document offers a snapshot capturing the current state of desertification and land degradation in Türkiye, alongside a comprehensive stakeholder analysis, an assessment of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, a review of the previous Strategy and Action Plan, and an outline of Türkiye’s vision and mission in combating desertification.

Document Title: A Low Carbon Pathway for the Aluminium Sector in the Republic of Türkiye
Family Title: A Low Carbon Pathway for the Aluminium Sector in the Republic of Türkiye
Family Summary:
This report, commissioned by the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Industry and Technology with the financial support of the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development, aims to lay the groundwork for the aluminium sector in Türkiye to accomplish green transformation in a manner that complies with Paris Agreement objectives. This project also serves to achieve Türkiye’s net zero target for 2053, and interim target as per its updated NDC. This includes laying the groundwork for Green Technology Roadmaps (to be prepared in 2023-2024 period).

The country has flourishing semi-aluminium processing operations with efficient yet very limited primary manufacturing. This study stands out as one of the initial ones to incorporate the modelling of semi-aluminium processing (remelting and refining) alongside primary aluminium production. This roadmap,can serve as foundation to developing investment plan and platform that helps to accelerate implementation of actions recommended by bringing together relevant actors and sharing a common vision for the sector. To bring the aluminium sector close to net zero emissions by 2053, the key decarbonisation levers identified by this study are: increased recycling (of aluminium), adoption of new, frontier technologies and transition to low-carbon energy.

The Roadmap recommends 21 actions that mainly focus on actions to be taken in the short term, but some can span over the entire timeframe up to 2050, across the areas of: vision and volume targets; regulatory and policy framework; financial and economic; health and safety; grid and port infrastructure; and supply chain.

Document Title: Environmental Improvement Plan
Family Title: Environmental Improvement Plan
Family Summary:
The Environmental Improvement Plan (EIP) is a strategic framework for improving England’s natural environment up to 2043, containing interim targets for the statutory Environment Act 2021 targets. It sets out how the government will work alongside individuals, communities and businesses to achieve England's nature ambitions in the context of nature depletion.

The EIP contains 10 goals on: the restoration of nature; the improvement of environmental quality through goals on air, water, chemicals and pesticides; driving forward a circular economy through goals on waste and resources; the achievement of environmental security through goals on climate, hazards and biosecurity; and increase to access to nature.

There is a focus on actions and investment to:

  • enhance the quantity and state of our critical natural capital assets;
  • capture more of the benefits from natural assets; and
  • reduce the pressures on our natural capital assets from direct use and respond to external threats.

Document Title: National Employment Strategy (2025-2028)

Family Summary:
The 2025-2028 National Employment Strategy (NES) and Action Plan aims not only to provide lasting solutions to labour market challenges but also to develop forward-thinking policies. Developed with broad stakeholder participation and centered around the principles of social dialogue, the National Employment Strategy seeks to enhance Türkiye's competitiveness and elevate social welfare. The strategy is built upon four fundamental policy pillars: improving green and digital transformation and skills alignment in labour markets, promoting inclusive employment, strengthening social protection employment relationship and improving sustainable employment in rural areas, each of which represents a key priority for Türkiye

It calls for the implementation of just transition policies to adapt to green and digital transformation in labour markets to sustain economic growth and improve worker well-being. For instance, in the field of agriculture, efforts will be supported to increase productivity per unit area and ensure a just transition to intensive agriculture, thereby enhancing resource efficiency and increasing rural employment.

It should also advance the green and digital transitions and make Member States’ economies and societies more resilient.The Total value reaches approx. €59.8 billion, which are divided into (i) €25.3 billion in RRF grants and (ii) €34.5 billion in RRF loans.

Family Title: Adaptation Roadmap to 2030
Family Summary:
Paraguay’s Adaptation Roadmap to 2030) serves as a practical guide to implement the country’s climate adaptation goals under its Updated NDCs and National Adaptation Plan (2022–2030). The roadmap outlines sectoral and cross-cutting adaptation actions, specifies the roles of institutions and subnational actors, and sets indicative timelines to strengthen resilience against climate impacts. Its purpose is to move beyond planning toward concrete, coordinated action at both national and local levels.

The document prioritises adaptation measures in key areas such as water management, cities, agriculture, health, ecosystems and biodiversity, energy, transport, and infrastructure, while also promoting governance, capacity building, and risk reduction. By clearly defining responsibilities and creating a framework for collaboration among stakeholders, the roadmap seeks to ensure that Paraguay is better prepared to face the risks of climate change and can build a more resilient, sustainable development pathway by 2030.

Document Title: Plan Maestro de Movilidad Eléctrica para El Transporte Público Urbano y Logístico de Paraguay (Multimodal Electric Mobility Master Plan for Urban Public Transport and Logistics)

Family Summary:
In 2023, the Multimodal Electric Mobility Master Plan for Urban Public Transport and Logistics in Paraguay was developed. This is a public policy tool complementary to the National Electromobility Strategy and will establish general and specific guidelines for a transition to the electrification of public transport and logistics in Paraguay. This comes as a commitment to supporting international efforts to reduce GHG emissions on the planet by replacing hydrocarbons with a clean energy source. At the same time, this transformation will allow Paraguay to take advantage of its 100% renewable generation matrix, reducing its dependence on petroleum derivatives.

The master plan has a vision to put Paraguay as a regional benchmark in promoting and driving electric mobility, with a sustainable, circular and comprehensive model, with 100% electric vehicles in public transport systems and 50% electric vehicles in logistics transport by 2040.

It integrates key elements from related planning tools, including the Indicative Programme for the Installation and Retirement of Power Plants (PIIRCE), and the expansion and modernisation programmes for the National Transmission Network (RNT) and General Distribution Networks (RGD). The PRODESEN aims to ensure universal access to electricity for over 125 million people, supporting social and economic development while addressing regional disparities. It prioritises the state-owned Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) in generation, transmission, and distribution, with plans to develop new power plants and modernise existing hydroelectric facilities, thereby reinforcing -according to the text- energy sovereignty and system reliability.The PRODESEN underscores Mexico’s commitment to international environmental agreements, including the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Paris Agreement, and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly focusing on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and promoting sustainable energy practices. It outlines a structured increase in clean and renewable energy generation, targeting a minimum of 35% of electricity from clean sources by 2024, as mandated by the Energy Transition Law (LTE) and the General Climate Change Law (LGCC). The programme includes planning for the integration of clean energy technologies, such as distributed generation, and emphasises energy efficiency and environmental protection, aiming a sustainable and orderly energy transition while maintaining system stability and affordability.

Document Title: The Vanuatu Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Policy 2022-2030
Family Title: The Vanuatu Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Policy 2016-2030
Family Summary: The Vanuatu Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Policy 2016-2030 was published by the Vanuatu government in combination with the Secretariat of the Pacific Community in 2015 to envision the country's response to climate change and make its communities resilient on the long term. The country initiated this process with the establishment of the National Advisory Board on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction in 2012. It is a broad set of measures based on accountability, sustainability, equity, community focus, collaboration, and innovation. The policy was updated in 2022 to incorporate the perspective of more recent climate-related policies across sectors. The policy insists on 1) establishing appropriate governance and strengthen institutional structures so they can effectively tackle the tasks they are pursuing, 2) to ensure that adequate resourcing is available for climate change and disaster risk reduction activities, notably via the implementation of entity accreditation and small grants schemes, 3) ensure that traditional knowledge and existing and new information such as data analysis, research and risk assessment are shared, 4) adaptation and disaster risk reduction, integrating the two targets and adopting community and ecosystem-based approaches to protect and economically assess losses, 5) low carbon development via an energy roadmap, renewable energy and energy efficiency, but also from a reduction in deforestation and land degradation, 6) and preparedness, planning, response and recovery to disasters by ensuring community awareness, early warning systems. The document also insists on capacity building, gender and social inclusion, multi-hazard approach and partnerships with a vast array of stakeholders. Implementation of the plan must be realised by integrating it into corporate and business plans, monitoring and evaluating the policy by the National Advisory Board on Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction (NAB), and reporting by NAB. A review of the current document should occur every three to five years to ensure it is in line with contemporary developments.

Document Title: Disaster Risk Management Plan
Family Title: Disaster Risk Management Plan
Family Summary:
The plan analyses how climate change, together with national socio-economic and demographic trends, contributes to disaster risk and population vulnerability in Bulgaria. Climate change is expected to have an overall negative impact. A general declining trend in precipitation is projected, with significant regional variation. In Eastern Bulgaria, average precipitation is expected to decrease by 5–10%, and in some areas by as much as 15–20%. Winters classified as cold under current climate conditions are expected to occur less frequently by the 2050s and to largely disappear by the 2080s, while hot summers are projected to become increasingly frequent.

Regional climate scenario models for Bulgaria estimate changes in air temperature and precipitation for two time horizons: the near future (2021–2050) and the distant future (2071–2100). Average annual air temperature is expected to increase by 1.6–3.1°C in the near future and by 2.9–4.1°C in the distant future. Over the coming decades, a steady increase in climate-related disasters, such as heat waves, droughts, heavy rainfall, and floods, is anticipated. With medium to high confidence, extreme heat, droughts, and forest fires are expected to intensify by 2050. While projections for precipitation-related hazards such as floods and landslides are more uncertain, recent trends of increasing precipitation intensity suggest that the frequency and severity of these events are also likely to rise by mid-century.

Family Summary:
Integrated pollution prevention and control (IPPC) refers to the minimising of pollution from various industrial sources throughout the EU. The Integrated Prevention Act, transposes EU legislation. The Act requires industrial and agricultural activities with a high pollution potential to obtain a permit; this permit can only be issued if certain environmental conditions are met so that the companies themselves bear responsibility for preventing and reducing any pollution they may cause.

The IPPC Directive is based on several principles, namely an integrated approach, best available techniques (BAT) flexibility and public participation.

In the area of GHG emissions, which are generated by the production and use of heat and electricity, the Act allows the regulator to apply the BAT concept, which should lead to increased energy efficiency of production. This Act also allows the application of emission limits or equivalent technical parameters, which are based on advanced technologies used in affected industrial sectors.

Family Summary:
This law indends to reduce greenhouse gas emissions within and outside Liechtenstein, and implement the EEA legislation on emissions trading. The targets are similar to EU commitments. Art. 4 states that the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is primarily pursued through domestic measures, in particular through energy, transport, environmental, forestry, agricultural, economic and financial measures. The Emission Trading Act anchors in law a GHG emission reduction target, reducing GHG emissions by 55% compared to the base year 1990.
